When there is nothing

The zero state is the one that matters most, because it is the claim the product makes every morning. It is not blank.

○ Nothing needs you, on either project.

Across all 2 bindings: every exception is dispositioned, every round in an open period is collected or explained, and no obligation is inside its warning window. The projects are named because “nothing” on a queue that spans an estate has to say what it spanned — a queue that had quietly narrowed to one site would show this same empty state. Search

/search

Identifier prefixes rank first — a practitioner searches by code, not by name.

Filtered bymatchesMW013 matches across 2 projects

Opening a result in another project switches your scope, and says so before it does.

Row-level security is fail-closed: you see MOCK-KRJ here because you hold a binding on it — Approver, where you hold Contributor at MOCK-WDL. Following one of its rows moves the whole application into that project: the header changes, the section strip changes, and so does what every other screen is about. A scope that changes silently is how somebody reads the wrong site’s numbers into a report. In this catalogue those rows stop at the switch, because MOCK-KRJ’s workspace is not drawn — the boundary is the honest place for a drawing of one project to end.

Why the second group ranks below the first

Both groups match the same query. The 5 above start with it; the 3 below contain it, because Kurrajong’s bores carry their project’s prefix — KRJ-MW03, not MW03.

Two sites under one customer will reuse a bore number eventually, and a register where only a column tells one MW03 from another is a register somebody will read wrong in a hurry. Prefixing the code is the cheap fix, and the cost of it is exactly this: the codes stop being prefix matches, and the ranking has to say so rather than quietly interleave them.

Projects

Every project you hold a role binding in, and what you are acting as on each one.

/projects

The role is on the row because “as what” is the first thing scope decides.

You are a Contributor at MOCK-WDL and an Approver at MOCK-KRJ — the same person, two sites, two sets of controls. As Approver you may sign a submission off and may not answer a review question; as Contributor the reverse. The controls that a binding does not carry are absent on that project rather than present and refusing, which is why the role has to be legible before you switch. A third role is bound on this project and sits on the Access register beside the others: Reader, held by S. Petrelli, who can read and export everything and write nothing.

Bindings resolve from Entra group membership, and membership is resolved from the directory on every request rather than read from the token — a snapshot taken at sign-in would leave somebody removed from a group working for the rest of the day. Every count below is taken from this project’s own records at build time — locations from the register, exceedances from the evaluation, overdue rounds from the programme.

MOCK-KRJ is real in the data and undrawn in this catalogue, and the row says which.

The second project carries four bores, four rounds and one criteria set — enough for the two questions a portfolio asks, and no more. What it does not carry is a workspace: there is no location register, no crosstab and no report of its own here, so its row opens the cross-project register that does hold its rows rather than linking into MOCK-WDL’s screens under another project’s name. Crossing a project boundary is a scope switch, not a link, and the switch is where this catalogue stops.

What the two rows say, read together

Two projects, one register. The rows interleave by date because that is how the week arrives — the oldest thing owed on this estate is a trigger response at Kurrajong that nobody was assigned, and it sits above every Wandalup row rather than below a project heading nobody opened.

MOCK-WDL is the noisy site and it is the well-run one: every exceedance on it is on a register, escalated to a TARP level and, where it obliged one, notified. MOCK-KRJ is quiet, and the quiet is the finding — one exceedance nobody has acknowledged in 199 days, and the round that would settle it overdue by 24 days. A site nobody opens looks fine from inside itself.

When you hold no bindings at all

Fail-closed row-level security means real users meet this state — on their first day, and again the morning after a group membership is revoked. It cannot dead-end.

○ You are signed in, and you hold no project bindings.

Strataflow reads your access from your organisation’s directory groups, not from a list kept here — so nobody at Strataflow can grant it, and neither can this screen. Your administrator adds you to a group like SG-Strataflow-<project>-Contributors; access appears on your next request, without signing in again. You are signed in as anakamura@wandalup.example on tenant wandalup.example.

A single-project customer never sees any of this

Most customers run one project. The switcher in the header collapses to the project name with no control on it, this screen is not linked from anywhere, and / lands on the project rather than here.

Switcher ceremony for a user with one thing to switch between is the kind of scaffolding that makes an internal tool feel like one. The URL still exists and still resolves; nothing in the architecture is special-cased, only what is shown.

This is not a dashboard

Every number here is a question somebody actually arrives with, and every one of them is a link to where it is answered. Nothing on this page exists to be looked at.

The distinction is load-bearing rather than stylistic: a decorative tile becomes stale without anybody noticing, because nobody was going to act on it. A tile that is the entrance to a queue is corrected the first morning it is wrong.

What a practitioner does from here, measured over the last quarter:

  • Opened an exceedance from the open list61%
  • Went straight to the import runs22%
  • Opened the programme11%
  • Read a number and did nothing6%
  • Tiles with no destination0

Recorded here so it can be checked against a real session rather than assumed. QB-8’s finish line is an unassisted practitioner, and no transcript shows one.

The tile that would be a dashboard here is a portfolio one — how are my other sites — and it is deliberately absent. This page cannot answer it without counting rows it does not own, so the question goes to Projects and Reporting obligations, which do.

1–19 of 19 locations

Class soil — the record a test pit keeps

5 of the 19 rows above are class soil, and none of them is a bore with its casing fields left blank. A bore is defined by what was built in it; a pit is defined by what was found in it — 18 logged depth intervals across 5 pits, each with the material, the moisture and the field screen that was read on it. The class decides which of those two records the location can legitimately carry, and the matrix of what comes out is recorded separately — which is why SW01, a surface-water location, has a sediment sample on this round.

Which interval went in the jar, and why that is a record

The plan fixed the rule before anybody stood at a pit: one discrete sample from the interval with the highest field screen, refusal horizons excluded, at any pit reading above 500 µS/cm. The background pit is submitted whatever it reads, because a control collected only when it is interesting is not a control.

TP04 is the row worth reading twice. It read 330 µS/cm at its best interval, below the threshold, so no discrete was submitted from it — and it contributed one increment to each of the two composite samples. It is a location on this register with no number of its own, and the reason is a rule that was written down in advance rather than a gap.

What the pit record does not have

No casing, no screen, no slot aperture, no annulus, no survey epoch history — and the register does not draw empty columns where a bore would have them. What it has instead is a log, a refusal depth and a backfill record.

The backfill row is not housekeeping. A pit is an excavation on an operating site and the reinstatement is what a tenement condition asks about; it belongs on the location record for the same reason a bore’s decommissioning does — the composite record and this one are the two halves of what happened at these five places.

The last row is the boundary and it is absolute. A register that starts growing result columns becomes a second crosstab that disagrees with the first, which is the failure this product exists to end.

Groups, and what changing one touches

Groups drive criteria applicability, programme membership and figure series, so a membership change is never only a label.

Adding MW07 to “Compliance boundary” would change:

  • Locations reassigned3 bores move from TSF to Compliance boundary
  • Criteria applicability changesLicence Table 4 begins applying to 3 bores
  • Historical evaluations affected0 — applicability is resolved at evaluation date, not re-run
  • Programmes touchedGW-QTR keeps all 3; GW-MTH loses 3
  • Figures whose series would change4 saved figure configurations name an area

Reversible. Group membership is audited with before and after state, and applicability is resolved at evaluation date — so nothing already evaluated moves.

Groundwater elevation is derived at the measurement date, never stored.

A depth-to-water reading taken in 2022 reduces through the 2019 datum; the same depth taken last week reduces through the 2024 one. Storing the elevation would freeze whichever datum happened to be in force the day it was calculated, and a resurvey would silently invalidate years of hydrograph.

Nest B — Borefield — this bore is half of a pair

MW03B is screened 46–52 m in the confined unit and MW01A 18–24 m in the superficial, at the same location. A register lists them as two rows; they are one installation, and the thing worth knowing is the difference between them.

The nest, read vertically.
BoreHydrostratigraphic unitScreened intervalStanding levelHeadEC
MW01ASuperficial18.0 – 24.0 m bgl11.42 m btoc203.40 m AHD840 µS/cm
MW03BConfined (Wandalup Sandstone)46.0 – 52.0 m bgl9.18 m btoc204.26 m AHD1120 µS/cm

Vertical gradient: Upward, +0.86 m from the confined unit to the superficial. The confined unit sits at higher head than the superficial one, so vertical leakage here is upward and TSF seepage in the superficial aquifer cannot be reaching the confined unit at this location. That is a containment argument, and it is only visible when the two bores are read as a nest rather than as two rows in a register.

Why this is not a footnote

A containment argument is made or lost on the vertical gradient, and it is invisible in every screen that treats a bore as a point. Two rows in a register, sorted alphabetically, with the number that matters being the difference between them.

How this bore is built

The screen sits wholly within the weathered granite, below a bentonite seal at 9.0–10.5 m. A sample from this bore represents the superficial aquifer at 12–18 metres and nothing above it, which is the claim every result from MW05 is interpreted under.

The string from surface to base, in the lengths it was installed in. The screened interval is its own row, not a kind of casing — it carries a unit and a slot aperture that no length of blank pipe has.

Casing material is a data-quality fact, not an inventory one.

50 mm Class 18 uPVC throughout. Steel casing contributes iron, manganese and zinc to a sample, so a metals exceedance in a galvanised-steel bore is a different conversation from the same number in a uPVC one — and this bore's is uPVC, which is one of the reasons the zinc result here is read as formation water.

Natural collapse is an answer, not a blank.

The interval below the filter pack is recorded as formation material falling back around the casing. Leaving it out would say the same thing as “nobody wrote it down”, and those are different facts (PP4).

The screened interval this instrument hangs in is the one above: at 15.62 m below top of casing the sensor sits inside 12.0–18.0 m of screen, which is what makes its water levels a measurement of the same aquifer the samples came from.

The series it is writingThe register and its deployment history

A continuous record and a quarterly one, held apart

This bore has 1,536 water levels from the logger over 2026-03-15 to 2026-05-31 and 38 rounds of results behind it. They are separate records and FR-1.10 says so: a logger has no analyte, no sample and no test, and putting the two in one table would mean inventing one of each.

The datum rule is the same rule, run more often. Groundwater elevation is derived at the measurement date and never stored — for a quarterly dip that is 38 derivations, and for this series it is 1,536, every one of them through the 2024-03-18 survey because that is the one in force. A resurvey tomorrow moves neither: it takes effect from its own epoch forward.

3 manual dips sit inside that window as well, and one of them found that 999 of the logger’s water levels had been derived under a wrong deployment depth. The dipper is not made redundant by a logger; it is what a logger is checked against.

Every QC sample names its parent by code. The incumbent alternative is a naming convention — MW05-DUP beside MW05, related by a substring and by nothing the database knows, and unrelated the moment somebody types MW05 DUP.

Every row in the matrix column reads Water, and until 2 September it did not. Eight rows said Groundwater, which is the location class of the bore rather than the material in the bottle, and three said Field blank, Trip blank and Equipment blank, which are sample types the QC-role column beside them already carries. The glossary’s list is closed at five — water, soil, sediment, vapour, biota — and it says the matrix is recorded rather than inferred from the place. The column was invisible while every sample on the project was water; it became legible the moment a round arrived carrying three matrices, which is the glossary’s own argument for why guessing it would be invisible when wrong.

38 containers across 11 samples — the same 38 the chain of custody sealed on 14 May and the same 38 the laboratory reconciled on arrival (38 of 38). Three screens, one addition: a manifest that cannot be added up to the number on the custody form is the first thing a challenge finds.

MW11 is not on this manifest, and that is the finding rather than an omission.

The 2026 Q2 window closed on 2026-05-14 in Australia/Perth and the bore yielded no sample — it is overdue by 10 days on the programme and short nine results on the data quality assessment. A manifest that quietly listed it, or that omitted the row without saying so, would let an overdue round read as collected. What the field record adds is why: the crew turned back at a flooded creek crossing on 13 May and found the bore dry on 14 May — and both dispositions are still on the tablet, which is precisely why the countdown is still running.

Three of the seven lines hold the round. A round marked complete with a bore outstanding is the failure the programme has named since the third pass, and the completion control refuses rather than being greyed out with no reason.

Two states, and they are not the same claim. The register above reads results-complete, which says every sample that was collected has its results back. This says the round is not complete, which is a fact about the field record — one disposition still on a tablet, one instrument with no post-round check. A product that ran the two together would let a round close because a laboratory finished.

The split is the point. A field duplicate and a laboratory duplicate are both duplicates and they are not the same control: one carries the act of collecting and the other does not, so a pair that disagrees says something different depending on which it was. Products that list them under one word have thrown away the only thing the pair was collected to separate.

The bench controls belong to the laboratory batch, not to this round — a control sample applies to a batch, which is what makes “which results does this failed spike qualify” answerable. The matrix spike on WDL-26Q2-005 is the one that failed, and it qualifies every zinc result in PAS-WO-268841 rather than the sample it was made from.

No composites on this round, and that is still true of every row above — each one is a discrete grab from a bore. Written 1 September 2026: “drawing a composite here would be drawing a matrix the slice does not carry.” Corrected 2 September 2026: the tsf seepage soil investigation below carries 2 of them, drawn as a proposal — additional matrices remain S8 widening in the PRD’s own sequencing, and drawing one does not move it.

2026-M05-SOIL — tsf seepage soil investigation

6–7 May 2026 · D. Okafor · Pilbara Analytical Services certificate PAS2026-04361 · matrices Soil, Sediment, Water · all times Australia/Perth

A different kind of round, and the record shape is different all the way down.

Sulfate, arsenic and zinc have all risen at MW05 over four quarters and the TSF is upgradient of it. A soil investigation on the seepage path asks a question groundwater cannot: whether the signature is in the unsaturated zone between the embankment and the bore, and at what depth. What it does not have is the groundwater round’s spine: there is no purge, no stabilisation series, no depth to water and no drawdown, because none of those describes a hole with no water in it. What it has instead is a depth-interval log written at each pit — 18 intervals across 5 pits, each with its material, its moisture and a field screen — and a rule fixed in advance for which interval goes in the jar. A soil round drawn as a groundwater round with the water columns blank would be the same defect as a test pit drawn as a bore missing its casing.

What this round has instead of a purge record

The groundwater round recordsThis round recordsWhy they are not the same record
Depth to water, dipped before the pumpDepth-interval log, horizon by horizonOne is a level in a hole; the other is what the hole is made of
Purge volume, rate and intake depthHow the pit was advanced, and its refusal depthNothing is purged. The excavation is the access
Stabilisation — five readings, three consecutive within toleranceField screen per interval — 18 readings, one per horizonStabilisation says the water is representative; the screen says which interval to submit
Filtration and preservation trainHomogenisation, and the equipment blank on itA composite is made with equipment, so the equipment needs a control
Drawdown against a low-flow limitBackfill and reinstatementThe excavation has to be put back, and that is a tenement condition

Both are field records and both answer “was this sample representative”. They answer it with different evidence, and a product with one screen for both would have to leave half of each blank.

Two link columns, and they are two different relations. Parent is FR-1.6’s — the QC sample made from another sample, one to one, and the glossary is explicit that it is mandatory for the types that have one and forbidden for the types that do not. Composite is FR-1.7’s — the sample this material was combined into, many to one. 4 rows carry the second and none carries the first, and running the two together would make a constituent increment read as a duplicate of the composite, which is close to the opposite of what it is.

23 containers across 13 samples — the same 23 the chain of custody sealed on 7 May and the same 23 reconciled on arrival. WDL-26M5-C02 contributes none of them: it was made at a laboratory bench four days after the cooler was sealed, so it has a sample identifier, five results and no containers at all. A manifest that gave it two to make the column tidy would have invented a journey.

Three samples, three matrices, and not one of them inferable from its place

SampleLocationLocation classMatrixWhat the pairing shows
WDL-26M5-S01TP01soilSoilThe ordinary case — class and matrix agree, which is why the distinction is invisible most of the time
WDL-26M5-D01SW01surface waterSedimentThe glossary’s own example: a location whose class is water yielding a sample whose material is not
WDL-26M5-QC1—no locationWaterA rinsate poured over an excavator bucket on a soil round. It has no location at all, and its matrix is water

The glossary puts it in one sentence — a groundwater location can yield a water sample and, on the same visit, a sediment one — and the consequence is the part worth drawing: the two are not evaluated against the same criteria and not held to the same holding times. Inferring the matrix from the class would have made WDL-26M5-D01 a water sample at a creek, assessed against a freshwater guideline, silently.

The quality control this round rests on

Two controls, and one of them is about the compositing itself.
ControlSampleParentWhat it answers
Field duplicate (blind)WDL-26M5-S03WDL-26M5-S02Sampling and analysis together, on soil — the only control that carries the act of collecting
Equipment blank (rinsate)WDL-26M5-QC1Excavator bucket and the stainless compositing bowl, rinsed after TP04 and before the creekIt is the only control on the compositing step.

The rinsate is the one that is particular to this round. Five increments went through one bowl and four through one splitter, so carry-over between increments would put the equipment inside the composite’s number; the blank is the only thing that says it did not, and every analyte on it is below the limit of reporting.

Recorded, not fixed: The limit applied is the round’s single field-duplicate limit. It was written for water and the data quality objectives carry no matrix dimension, so a soil duplicate is held to a water number. That is stricter rather than looser — soil is heterogeneous at the scale of a trowel and the conventional soil limit is wider — so nothing passes here that would fail a soil limit. Giving the objectives an applicability rule by matrix is a versioned change to them, with an effective date, and it is not something this investigation makes on its way past.

The composites, their increments and the honest limitThe pits and their depth intervalsThe soil results

A blind duplicate stays blind, and the link is still recorded

Two field duplicates this round — WDL-26Q2-004 and WDL-26Q2-008 — and the laboratory was told about neither. The link exists in the record from the moment the sample was collected, so the RPD can be computed, and the laboratory never had the chance to make two results agree.

The distinction the screen has to keep is between the laboratory did not know and we do not know. Showing the parent here is correct; showing it on anything the laboratory receives is not.

FR-3.10 asks that the barometric source be defined per location group, so the importer does not ask which barometer to use: it resolves the source in force for TSF downgradient compliance on the file’s own dates, and records it on every water level it derives. An importer that offered a barometer picker would be offering a way to compensate one bore against the wrong sky.

The vendor and the extension are MOCK, shaped like a real one. A format that is obviously invented cannot be judged, and one that is not obviously fictional is a screenshot waiting to be mistaken for somebody’s real deliverable.

The format is chosen, never defaulted.

A deliverable read with the wrong format parses to zero rows and every downstream screen then says, truthfully, that nothing is waiting. The importer states how many rows it read before anything else happens.

Before — what the control says it will do

Committing IMP-0239 writes, in one transaction:

Reversible. A committed run can be withdrawn, which removes its results from every register that counted them and leaves the reversal itself on the record — a reversal is an event, not an erasure.

The counts come from the staged data rather than from this screen, and they are the same numbers the receipt below will report. A commit control that does not say what it will write is asking for a signature on a blank page.

The laboratory reported −999, which their format defines as analysis aborted. That is not a concentration, and there is no value here to accept, qualify or estimate. Storing it as a number would invent a measurement; storing it as zero would invent a clean result.

A parameter is holding when the spread across the three readings in the window — largest minus smallest — sits inside its tolerance, taken against their mean where the tolerance is a percentage. Every flag in the last column is computed from the numbers to its left rather than recorded beside them, which is the difference between a stabilisation record and a note saying the bore stabilised. The looser reading of ± 3% — each reading within 3% of the mean — allows twice the movement and would have called this bore stable one reading earlier.

A large disagreement between the two means the sample changed between the bore and the bench — degassing, a temperature artefact, or a mislabelled container — and it is worth catching before the whole suite is interpreted. It is a consistency check that costs nothing and nobody runs it.

The percentage is computed from the two numbers beside it. A difference typed next to two values it does not follow from is the commonest way a check like this survives being wrong.

What “did not stabilise” actually means here

Five of the six parameters held: ph, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, redox, temperature were all inside tolerance at the last reading. Turbidity never was — it stayed above 10 NTU for every one of the 14 readings and moved by more than ± 10% across every window of three, which is a bore mobilising fines rather than a bore settling.

Stabilisation is reported per parameter as well as overall, because a purge recorded only as “not stabilised” tells a reviewer nothing about which measurement to distrust. Here it is exactly one, and it is the one that decides whether a filtered metal reads high.

MW0914 readings · 22.0 L

Turbidity would not settle. Purged 22.0 L over 71 minutes and stopped: every other parameter had held for an hour and the crew had two bores left before the cooler had to leave for the courier.

Total depth was dipped at this bore and nowhere else this round: Dipped because turbidity would not fall — 0.6 m of silt above the surveyed base, recorded against the location.

Qualifier T carried to every metal result from this sample

A judgement, recorded as one

The field officer sampled anyway, which is the right call at a remote bore on a day rate — and the record makes it a stated judgement rather than an invisible one. A product that only accepted stabilised samples would simply have no record of this bore at all.

The series outcome is one of three words and this is the second: Stable · Sampled by judgement · Purged dry. It travels with the sample: QA/QC reads it as the stabilisation check, and the qualifier it produced is applied by rule rather than by anybody deciding case by case.

The cracked bottle is why MW09 is one result short, and it is recorded here rather than appearing later as an unexplained gap in the crosstab. The nitrate warning is why the holding-time failure that followed was foreseeable rather than a surprise.

Chain of custody

Custody is a chain, not a PDF

A signed form scanned into a folder proves a form was signed. It does not answer the question a challenge actually asks: was this sample ever unaccounted for.

Every transfer above is a row with a time, two parties and a seal number, so an unbroken chain is a query rather than somebody reading four pages of handwriting. The one exception in it is marked as an exception and carries forward to the result it affected.

Chain of custody — 2026-Q2-GW

Every hand that held these samples, from the bore to the laboratory bench.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. The PRD names no chain-of-custody surface, and there is no route for one.

FR-1.6 gets the samples as far as the event and FR-3.8 picks them up at the certificate; the days in between are where a defensibility argument is actually won or lost. Receipt and custody draws the laboratory end of the chain because that is where the record used to start — which is the tell. A chain reconstructed afterwards from a scanned form proves that a form was signed; it does not answer the question a challenge asks, which is whether these samples were ever unaccounted for. This screen argues for itself and is filed under Sampling events on that argument. It is called Chain of custody rather than eCOC because the glossary has an entry for custody transfer and none for the acronym: practitioners call the paper form a COC and the electronic one an eCOC, and both words are named here once rather than becoming the product’s (QB-9).

The rows are ordered by sequence rather than by time — two handovers can share a recorded minute, and a chain ordered only by the clock closes silently over a missing link. Here they run 1 to 7 with nothing missing between them, and that is the property worth having: a gap in the sequence is a hole somebody has to explain, where a gap in a list of timestamps is invisible. The last four rows are the ones Receipt and custody has always drawn — they are the same four rows, read from the same record, not a second copy of them.

Sealing a cooler and handing it over — what that writes, before you do it:

  • Transfers appended1 — appended, never edited
  • Containers committed to the consignment38 across 11 samples
  • Seal numbers frozen onto the transfer4471, 4472
  • Samples that can still be added to this chain0 — a sealed cooler is closed
  • Rows that can be corrected afterwards0 — a correction supersedes and both entries stay readable

Not reversible in the ordinary sense. A transfer cannot be edited or deleted; a mistake is corrected by a superseding entry that names what it corrects, and both stay on the record. That is what makes the chain evidence rather than a document.

One seal number, written down twice, differently

Seal number on the second cooler lid — the field record says 4472 and the laboratory’s receiving form says 4427.

Seal 4471 and the temperature check agree. Nothing about the containers is in doubt; the identity of one seal is. Both seals were found intact, which is a different check and it passed. The product has not chosen between the two numbers and will not: a transposition is the likeliest reading, and the likeliest reading is exactly what a custody challenge attacks.

Where this record stops, and what picks it up

This screen owns the chain: raising it in the field, the containers it accumulates, the seals, every transfer up to and including the handover the laboratory signs for, and the one below that continues past it. It owns the discrepancy above, because a disagreement about a seal is a custody question.

Receipt and custody owns what the laboratory found when it opened the box — cooler temperature, preservation, breakages, holding time on arrival — and the results those explain. The cracked sulfate bottle is its finding, not this one’s.

After that the round leaves custody altogether and becomes a deliverable: the certificate and the rows that come back are Import runs. Three screens, one seam each, and each seam named on both sides of it.

What arrived, and in what conditionThe field round that filled it

Where the chain continues — the subcontracted fraction

Pilbara Analytical Services holds no NATA scope for USEPA 1633. The PFAS fraction is subcontracted, and the subcontract laboratory issues its own certificate. One naming convention to read past: PAS-WO-268841 is the submission work order — the number the whole box travels under — and PAS also reports its metals run under it, so the same identifier names this bottle’s physical origin and the metals batch on the QA/QC screen. Yarra Regional issues its own batch, YAR-B-118420, which is why a PFAS result never cites the metals number. So one container leaves Pilbara Analytical Services again, and the record does not stop at the first laboratory door.

Chain MOCK-COC-2026Q2-014-S1, a continuation of MOCK-COC-2026Q2-014. Its own sequence, because it is its own chain — and a reader following a PFAS result arrives here rather than at a gap.

A round with no chain yet

○ 2026-Q3-GW has no chain of custody, because it has not been collected.

There are 6 rounds on this project and 5 of them have one. This is the other: planned, with a window, a location list and an analyte suite, and no samples yet. That is a different sentence from no rounds have ever been sampled, and a screen printing “No data” for both would have said nothing in either case. The chain is raised at the first bore, on the device, before the first container is filled — not typed up afterwards from a notebook. Raising one writes an empty record attributed to you, and it can be discarded until the first transfer is signed.

Instruments and loggers

Every instrument on this project: where it is, when it was last calibrated, and what it has been recording.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. The instrument is the first step of a journey the product defers, and nothing owns it.

FR-1.10 and FR-3.10 are marked S8 in the PRD and that marking stands — drawing this does not reschedule it. What the drawing is for is the step before the data: a water level is only as good as the instrument that wrote it, the depth that instrument was hanging at, and the date it was last calibrated, and those three facts have lived in a field officer’s notebook on every project any of us has worked on. The completion preflight on Field capture has counted these instruments since the field round was drawn; this is the register it counts. The word instrument here means a device. The glossary uses it for a statutory instrument — the licence an operation is held to — and both senses are in the PRD, so this screen names which one it means rather than minting a third word for the other.

The series these intervals hold up

An interval record can say “from here to there”; only a check can say “and nothing else covered that bore in between”. A deployment history that quietly overlaps is how two instruments come to claim the same hour, and the water levels from that hour then have two provenances and no way to choose between them.

The shape is real — a hire company’s serial, a model, a full-scale accuracy — because a register whose fields are obviously invented cannot be judged.

Deployment history

A logger is not at a bore. It was at a bore over a span, at a stated depth, and the span is what makes a water level from March mean something different from one in May. So a deployment is an interval record in the same shape as a location survey: dated, never edited, and superseded rather than overwritten when it turns out to be wrong.

The barometric source, per location group

FR-3.10 asks for barometric compensation from a defined source per location group, and that is a record rather than a setting. A location group is the glossary’s: a named set of locations assessed together, where membership is an assessment decision rather than a place. The source has a span, because it changed — MOCK-BL-01 replaced MOCK-BL-02 on 1 April 2025, and a water level from 2024 was compensated against a barometer 6.4 km away whether or not anybody remembers it.

Why the station’s elevation is on this table

Atmospheric pressure falls with height, so a barometer standing 12.8 m above the water surface at MW05 does not read the pressure that surface is under. The compensation rule carries the difference — 0.1525 kPa, which is 0.0156 m of water.

Fifteen millimetres. It is carried anyway, and stating why is the point: a rule that drops a term because it is small on this site is a rule that drops it on the site where it is not. The inputs and the constant ride on every water level the rule produces (PP3), so the arithmetic can be re-done rather than trusted.

The reference elevation is the round’s own dipped level, held constant for the deployment. Re-deriving it from the level being computed would make the rule circular, and a rule that depends on its own output is one nobody can check.

Where the register is honest about what it does not cover

4 of the monitored bores and instrumented points have never had an instrument in them: MW01A, MW03B, MW11, MW12. That is a fact about the network rather than a hole in this register, and it is on the screen because a register that lists only what it holds cannot be used to ask what is missing.

MW11 is the one worth reading twice. It is a compliance-boundary bore, it was dipped twice this round and found dry, and a pressure transducer in a dry bore records atmosphere. Its group has a barometric source and no instrument to compensate — the record is coherent because the source is defined against the group, not against a device that happens to be in a hole.

Redeploying an instrument — what it writes

Closing one interval and opening another, with a new sensor depth. It does not touch a single pressure reading: every water level already derived keeps the depth it was derived under, and the new depth applies from the hour the instrument went back in. Getting that backwards would silently re-date years of series.

Logger series — MW05

One bore’s continuous water level: what the instrument wrote, what the rule made of it, and what correcting it reached.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. FR-1.10 and FR-3.10 are marked S8, and drawing them does not move them.

The requirement is two sentences and both of them are structural: a series from a logger is held separately from discrete results, and raw and corrected are retained independently. A product that stores only the corrected series has thrown away the ability to re-correct it when the compensation turns out to have been given a wrong number — which is exactly what happened at this bore, and it is on this screen because the raw record survived it.

Raw is retained. Corrected is derived.

The instrument is a non-vented absolute transducer: it measures the pressure above it, which is the water plus the atmosphere on top of the water. The number it writes is 175.532 kPa at the first hour of this file, and that number is never edited by anything on this screen. Everything else here is computed from it.

The rule, its constants and its inputs — carried on every water level it produces (PP3).
StepWhat it doesInput
1 · Elevation offsetThe barometer stands at 212.4 m AHD and the water surface at 199.64 m AHD, so the pressure at the water surface is higher by that difference times the lapse rate.0.01195 kPa/m → +0.1525 kPa
2 · CompensateSubtract the barometric pressure at the bore from the recorded total pressure.MOCK-BL-01, hourly
3 · Water columnConvert the remainder to metres of water.9.804 kPa per metre at 4 °C
4 · Depth to waterSubtract the column from the sensor’s depth below the measuring point.15.62 m, from the deployment record
5 · Groundwater elevationSubtract the depth to water from the top of casing in force on the day the water level was measured — the 2024-03-18 survey, not the current one.208.11 m AHD

Step 5 is ADR-0015 running once an hour. Groundwater elevation is derived at the measurement date and never stored — the same rule the bore’s own screen states for a quarterly dip. Storing 1,536 elevations would freeze one survey into the record, and the correction that reaches back through a resurvey would find nothing it could move.

Held separately from the results, which is the requirement

This bore contributed 1,536 water levels and 0 results to the record over this window. The results it does have came from the round — one sample, on one morning, with an analyte suite behind it.

They are not the same kind of thing and a product that put them in one table would have to invent an analyte for a water level and a sample for an hour. FR-1.10’s “separately from discrete results” is a schema decision that shows up here as two screens, two counts, and two marks on one plate.

The dipper is not replaced

3 manual dips sit on this plate as filled diamonds. One of them — 2026-04-14 08:05 — is the only water level this bore has for the fortnight the instrument was in the workshop, and it exists because somebody drove out and dipped the bore knowing the logger was gone.

Six water levels, reproducible with a calculator

Every column but the first two is derived, and the derivation closes at the rounding the instrument reports. (raw − barometric at bore) ÷ 9.804 is the column; sensor depth minus the column is the depth to water; top of casing minus that is the elevation.

Raw on the left, retained. Everything to the right of it is computed from it.

The gap, and why it is drawn as one

14 days with no water level

From
2026-04-06 09:00 AWST

2026-04-20 09:00 AWST
Hours with no record
336
Because
Removed for service — Scheduled twelve-month service. Retrieved 09:00 AWST; the bore has no continuous record from that hour.
Back in the bore
2026-04-20 · A. Nakamura

The trace breaks rather than crossing it. A polyline over 336 missing hours asserts 336 water levels nobody measured — which is the rule the hydrograph has stated since the third pass and this is the first plate in the catalogue with the data to draw it.

The gap is computed from the deployment interval the service record closes and reopens. A gap that did not line up with a service record could not be drawn here, because there is nothing else for it to be made of.

What was in the bore instead

Nothing. No second logger was deployed, and the register’s interval check says so: for those 336 hours MW05 has no deployment at all.

What it does have is one water level — 2026-04-14 08:05 AWST, 8.39 m below top of casing, dipped by D. Okafor. The check against the logger for that dip is refused rather than computed: the nearest logged water level is a week away on either side, and a residual measured across a week is a number that looks like a check and is not one.

A gap is not a flat line and it is not a zero

The two failure modes are opposite and both are common: interpolating across the gap invents a record, and filling it with zero invents a dry bore. What happened is that nobody measured, and the only honest rendering of that is nothing.

Findings on the series

The test is the one QA/QC uses on a result that looks wrong against its own history — a modified z-score over the 1,534 hourly changes in depth to water, median 0.0000 m and median absolute deviation 0.0020 m, flagged above 3.5. It is never taken across the gap: a fortnight of absence is not a step. It found 2, and they end differently.

MOCK-FIND-LS-01

◐unresolved

2026-05-04 03:00 → 2026-05-04 07:00 AWST · 5 hours · 6 water levels · score 65.8

Water level rose 0.382 m over 5 hours and returned. Atmospheric pressure moved 0.138 kPa over the same hours — 0.014 m of water, and the wrong way to explain it.

Raised, not resolved. A pressure step with no barometric counterpart is a recharge pulse, a slug of water down the annulus, or the instrument. The product does not choose between them, and the corrected series does not smooth it away: a correction that removes what it cannot explain has destroyed the evidence for the explanation.

MOCK-FIND-LS-02

●dispositioned

2026-05-13 09:00 → 2026-05-13 11:00 AWST · 3 hours · 4 water levels · score 14.2

Water level fell 0.042 m and recovered, across the hours the purge log covers.

The field record has this bore purged at 0.24 L/min from 08:02 to 08:40 on 2026-05-13, with a recorded drawdown of 0.06 m. The logger recorded the same event the field sheet describes, from a different instrument. Dispositioned by rule against the field record — not by anyone deciding case by case.

The anomaly is not smoothed, and it is not an exceedance

The correction re-derived every water level in its reach — including these 6. The spike is still 0.382 m and still there, because a compensation rule is not a filter. Removing what it cannot explain would destroy the evidence for the explanation, and the thing that most needs explaining is the thing most likely to be removed. One coincidence to read past: the spike's 0.382 m and the correction's 0.38 m shift are near-identical magnitudes with no shared cause — one is water moving at the screen over five hours, the other a sensor re-seated deeper and applied as a constant to every level in the reach. Neither is an artefact of the other.

The barometric record is what makes it a finding rather than weather: pressure moved 0.138 kPa over the same hours, which is 0.014 m of water and the wrong sign to explain a rise.

It is in the raw record, not in the correction. The instrument wrote 168.363 kPa at 2026-05-04 02:00 and 172.023 kPa at 2026-05-04 04:00 — a rise of 3.660 kPa, which is 0.373 m of water before anything was done to it. Both traces on the plate move with it, which is what the raw trace is drawn for: an event that appeared in only one of them would be an artefact of the rule, and this is not one.

An anomaly is not an exceedance. This is a movement in a bore’s own record, and nothing on the exceedance register moves because of it. A fixed limit says the water is out of compliance; a bore’s own history says something changed. Both can be true and neither is the other.

The one that resolved, and what resolved it

MOCK-FIND-LS-02 was dispositioned by rule against a record that already existed: the purge log has this bore pumped at 0.06 m of drawdown from 08:02 to 08:40 on 2026-05-13, and the logger felt it.

Two instruments, one event, agreeing. That is the strongest thing a QA record can say and it costs nothing but keeping both.

The sensor depth was recorded as 16.00 m below top of casing when the instrument went back in the bore. The cable mark and the redeployment record say 15.62 m. Every corrected water level from that hour onward was 0.38 m too deep.

The 2026-05-13 08:37 dip read 8.47 m btoc and the series read 8.84 m — 0.37 m apart, against a ±0.05 m acceptance. A logger that agrees with a dipper is checked; one that does not is what a check is for.

The 2026-05-13 08:37 row is the one that raised the correction, and the offset column is why it is a fair comparison rather than a coincidence: the dip was read at the end of purging and the nearest logged water level is 23 minutes later, on a bore recovering from 0.06 m of drawdown. The residual after correcting is -0.011 m. A capture time and a comparison time are different questions and the table asks both.

What the correction re-evaluated — and what it did not

This series is a water level. Every exceedance on this project is a concentration.

Re-evaluation is the sixth step of the telemetry journey and the honest answer is narrow: correcting 999 water levels moved nothing on the exceedance register, because all 9 of its rows are chemistry — arsenic, zinc, nickel, copper, PFAS, pH, conductivity, nitrate — evaluated against concentration criteria that a water level is not an input to. Saying so is more useful than inventing an impact: a screen that reported “9 exceedances re-evaluated” after a level correction would be teaching a reader to distrust every impact statement it makes.

What a corrected level series does reach, counted:

  • Water levels re-derived through the rule999
  • Groundwater elevations re-derived with them999 — derived, never stored, so they move with it
  • The hydrograph trace over the corrected spanmoves 0.38 m
  • Control heads on the potentiometric surface0 — the 2026 Q2 fit is made of manual dips at the round
  • Exceedances, TARP levels, notifications0 — none of them takes a water level as an input
  • Raw pressure readings altered0

Reversible in the only sense that matters: the raw record is intact, so the series can be re-derived under any deployment depth, any barometric source and any version of the rule. That is the whole argument for retaining raw and corrected independently, and it is the argument this bore proved.

Why the potentiometric surface does not move

The 7-point fit on the map is built from the round’s manual dips, one per bore, taken within three days of each other. This correction reaches a continuous series at one bore and does not touch the dip that bore contributed — which is why the answer is zero rather than small.

It would not always be. A fit built from logged levels at an instant would move by 0.38 m at this bore, and the bearing and gradient with it. The reason to state which inputs a surface has is that the answer to “did this reach the flow direction” depends entirely on it.

MW11 contributes no head to that fit either, for a different reason: it was dipped to the base of its screened interval and found dry. A dry bore is a fact about the aquifer, not a gap in the record, and it is drawn on the plate without a head.

Composite sample

A sample made of other samples — the increments it holds, the decision that combined them, and what that decision cost.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. FR-1.7 asks for composites with traceability to constituent increments, and the increment-to-composite step has never had a record here.

Soil and sediment are two of the nine location classes the product has carried since S1, and additional matrices are S8 widening in the PRD’s own sequencing — drawing this does not reschedule it. What the drawing is for is the act in the middle: 9 positions were sampled and 2 analyses were run, and everything that makes that a defensible saving rather than a lost record — which positions, at what depth, on what scheme, decided by whom, and what can no longer be said afterwards — lives between the field sheet and the certificate. FR-1.7 names three matrices and this investigation carries two: there is no soil-gas programme on this site, so vapour is not drawn rather than invented.

2composite samples
9constituent increments
2 of 9analyses run for those positions
2positions with no number of their own
10 daysleft to buy the resolution back

What compositing buys, and what it costs

What it buys — coverage

9 positions covered by 2 analyses. Discrete coverage of the same ground would have cost 9; 7 were not run. That is the whole argument for a composite and it is a real one: an investigation budget is a fixed number of analyses, and spending them on one point each buys precision about points nobody asked about.

Coverage is what an average over an area is for. C01 answers what is the surface of the toe seepage area like, which is the question a rehabilitation decision is taken over, and no single pit answers it at all.

What it costs — resolution, and it is not recoverable by arithmetic

A result on a composite cannot be attributed to one increment. Not is difficult to; cannot. The material was combined before it was measured, so the number describes the combination and there is nothing smaller inside it to recover. No rule, no re-derivation and no statistical treatment gets it back — the information was never recorded, because it was never created.

2 of the positions sampled have no number of their own at all: Grid node G3 and TP04. They are covered and they are not resolved, and the register says so on their own rows.

The cost has a size, and it is arithmetic rather than a caution. For a quantity carried in the mass, a composite of n increments reading v is consistent with one increment at n × v and the rest at zero; and an increment carrying less than n × the reporting limit contributes less than the limit and disappears inside it. Both numbers are computed from the composite’s own value and its increment count — nothing here is a rule of thumb.

What WDL-26M5-C02’s value leaves open about any one of its 4 increments.
AnalyteComposite readsAny one increment could be as high asAn increment below this is invisible in it
Sulfate1180 mg/kg4,720 mg/kg — 4 × the composite, if every other increment were zero80 mg/kg — 4 × the 20 mg/kg reporting limit
Arsenic9.1 mg/kg36.4 mg/kg — 4 × the composite, if every other increment were zero8 mg/kg — 4 × the 2 mg/kg reporting limit
Zinc49 mg/kg196 mg/kg — 4 × the composite, if every other increment were zero20 mg/kg — 4 × the 5 mg/kg reporting limit

pH and EC are not on this table, and leaving them off is the same discipline as the rest of the screen. The bound holds for a quantity that is conserved when masses are combined — milligrams of sulfate per kilogram add up. A pH and the conductivity of a 1:5 extract are properties of the combined material rather than sums over it, so n × their value is not a bound on anything, and printing one would be inventing arithmetic to fill a row.

The discrete samples do not bound this. TP01 reads 2140 mg/kg of sulfate — but at 0.90 – 1.60 m, which is a different depth interval from the 0.30 – 1.10 m this composite covers. A number from another horizon is not a constraint on this one, and treating it as one is the mistake a depth axis exists to prevent.

Two composites, and the difference is where they were made

Both were fixed by the same plan on the same day and both use the same scheme. One was mixed in a bowl at the pit and one at a laboratory bench, and that single fact decides whether the resolution above is gone or merely unbought.

The same decision taken twice, in two places, with two different consequences.

It is worth saying plainly which one is better, because the record should not be neutral about it: laboratory compositing keeps a door open that field compositing closes, at the cost of freighting four bags instead of one. Field compositing is still right where the increments are genuinely interchangeable and the question is an average — which is what WDL-26M5-C01 was collected to answer. What is not defensible is doing it in the field without knowing that the increments cannot be recovered, and that is the sentence this screen exists to put in front of somebody.

The compositing decision, as a record

Who, when, on what scheme, and why — four questions a regulator asks about a composite and a filename cannot answer. The scheme was fixed in the plan before the field work and the act was performed afterwards, so both are recorded and they are not the same event: one is a decision with an approver, the other is a physical act with an operator and a minute.

A composite is not a derived value

The distinction, and why it is not pedantry

Derived. A derived value is arithmetic over other results. It keeps its components and the versioned rule that produced it, it can be recomputed, and it never overwrites what the laboratory reported (FR-2.1, FR-2.3, FR-2.4). PFOS + PFHxS on MW05 is one.

Composite. A composite result is a number the laboratory reported on a physical sample. The combining happened to the material, before any measurement existed, so there are no component results to keep and nothing to recompute. What it carries instead is the compositing scheme, the increments and their positions.

A product that filed a composite under derivation would offer to re-derive it, would show a rule version that does not exist, and would imply the increments have numbers behind them. All three are false, and the third is the one that would mislead a regulator.

Which is why the word is scheme

The domain already spends rule on the derivation engine — a versioned artefact with inputs, an effective date and a recomputable output. Reusing it here would import all four of those promises onto something that keeps none of them.

Derivation ruleCompositing scheme
Acts onResultsMaterial
HappensAfter measurementBefore it
RecomputableYes, from the inputsNo — there are no inputs to recompute from
KeepsComponents and a rule versionIncrements, their positions and their intervals
VersionedYes, with an effective dateFixed per composite, in the sampling plan

Both live on the same lineage screen, one chain each, and the shapes are deliberately not interchangeable there either.

Traceability, and it has to run both ways

FR-1.7 asks for traceability to constituent increments. One direction is the easy one and it is not the one a challenge uses.

Backward — result → composite → increments, and the one question with no answer

1180 mg/kg Sulfate as SO₄ (1:5 soil:water) · sample WDL-26M5-C02 · certificate PAS2026-04361 · 0.30 – 1.10 m across 4 positions
What this number can say
  • The 4 positions it covers, each with its own depth interval and its own coordinate.
  • The envelope those intervals span — 0.30 – 1.10 m — and that they are not identical, so the composite has a nominal interval rather than an exact one.
  • That the scheme was equal mass, so no position is weighted above another.
  • That the increments are retained, and until when.
What it cannot say, and will not pretend to

Which of the 4 carried it. The material was combined before it was measured, so the number describes the combination and nothing smaller.

There is no qualifier for this and no confidence figure that would help. The honest rendering of “which increment” is a refusal with a reason, and the reason is that the question was foreclosed by an act somebody took deliberately and recorded above.

Buying the resolution back

The decision, and the clock on it

Which of the four increments carries the sulfate in WDL-26M5-C02? There is an answer and it has a price and a deadline. Both are on the record rather than in somebody’s head, which is the difference between a decision and a thing that quietly stops being possible.

The holding time is per analyte suite, and the shortest one binds the decision.
SuiteWindowUsed on the compositeExpiresLeft as at 2026-05-24
1:5 soil:water extract — pH, electrical conductivity, sulfateExtracted within 28 days of collection, held at ≤ 6 °C28 days5 of 282026-06-0310 days
Total metals — arsenic, zincDigested within 180 days of collection, held at ≤ 6 °C180 days6 of 1802026-11-02162 days

Analysing the 4 retained increments for the 1:5 soil:water extract suite would:

  • Analyses purchased4 — one per retained increment
  • Material consumedPart of the 750 g held for each; the remainder stays in the store
  • New results4 × 3 on the extract suite — none of which supersedes the composite; it stays exactly what it is
  • What it would answerWhich of the four positions carries the sulfate, and whether TP04 carries any of it
  • What it cannot answerAnything about the surface composite — those five increments no longer exist

The window is not reversible and nothing here can extend it. 10 days remain on the 1:5 soil:water extract suite; after 2026-06-03 the same analysis returns a number with a holding-time qualifier on it rather than an answer. The purchase itself is ordinary and can be cancelled until the laboratory opens a jar.

And the position that has nothing else

TP04 is where this stops being an abstraction. Its best field screen read 330 µS/cm, below the plan’s 500 µS/cm threshold, so no discrete sample was submitted from it. It contributed one increment to each composite and it has no result of its own on any surface in this product.

That is a defensible design — a threshold written in advance and applied — and it is also the exact circumstance in which somebody later asks “what was TP04?” and gets an answer only if the increment is still in a jar. It is, until 2026-06-03.

The equipment blank is the control on the compositing step

Five increments through one bowl and four through one splitter. If either carried material between them, the composite is partly a number about the equipment. WDL-26M5-QC1 — matrix Water, on a soil round — says it did not: every analyte below the limit of reporting.

The field duplicate, and the limit it was judged against

WDL-26M5-S03 is a blind duplicate of WDL-26M5-S02. Worst relative percent difference across the four ratioed analytes: 7.1%, against a limit of ≤ 30%; pH differs by 0.1 of a unit and is not ratioed at all.

Recorded, not fixed: The limit applied is the round’s single field-duplicate limit. It was written for water and the data quality objectives carry no matrix dimension, so a soil duplicate is held to a water number. That is stricter rather than looser — soil is heterogeneous at the scale of a trowel and the conventional soil limit is wider — so nothing passes here that would fail a soil limit. Giving the objectives an applicability rule by matrix is a versioned change to them, with an effective date, and it is not something this investigation makes on its way past.

The containers, on the same chain as anything else

A composite’s containers travel like any sample’s, so this is the chain of custody’s own record rather than a parallel one — same shape, same sequence discipline, same reconciliation against the manifest. MOCK-COC-2026M5-009 · 6 transfers · 23 containers, which is the manifest’s own sum and not a second number beside it.

Ordered by an explicit sequence, not by time — a chain with a gap in its numbering is visible where one ordered by clock silently closes over it.

Two things this chain does that the groundwater one did not need to

It carries an instruction. Composite instruction written on the form at dispatch: combine 250 g from each of WDL-26M5-I01 to I04 into WDL-26M5-C02, equal mass, and retain the balance of each. Written by D. Okafor under Sampling and analysis plan — TSF toe seepage investigation, rev 1, approved by R. Whitmore on 2026-05-04.

And the compositing act is deliberately not on it. The glossary’s custody transfer is one handover of a set of samples from one party to another; the bench work at 2026-05-11 10:15 AWST moved nothing between parties. Appending it would have quietly made this chain read seven hops long and turned a laboratory operation into a custody event. It is recorded above, with its own operator and its own minute.

PAS-WO-268503
How the laboratory end of a chain is drawn

What any of this was assessed against

Nothing, and that is the honest answer rather than an oversight. Applicability is by matrix among other things, the criteria library holds 5 sets, and 0 of them carry a soil or sediment matrix — every one is freshwater or groundwater. So every result in this investigation is not evaluated, computed from the library rather than assumed.

Two different roads reach that state and this product keeps them apart. A sample whose matrix nobody stated gets there because nothing could be selected — a road nobody can close. A sample whose matrix is stated and for which the library holds no set gets there because of a configuration decision, and that one somebody can close: a soil criteria set is a deliberate change on the criteria library, with an effective date, an applicability rule and a version. This investigation does not make it in passing.

What a practitioner says instead is a comparison against the site’s own background, and it is an interpretation rather than an outcome — it gets no mark on the results grid and it makes nothing an exceedance.

Recorded, not fixed: The library’s matrix column is not holding matrix words. Freshwater is an ANZG receptor and Groundwater is a location class, and neither is one of the glossary’s five — so this count is a match over strings rather than over a field, and it is right by inspection rather than by construction. Splitting that column into the dimensions it carries at once is a versioned change to the criteria library with an effective date on every set, and it is recorded rather than made here.

The soil grid, every cell not evaluatedAgainst background

The figure this investigation wants is not drawn, and this is the record of why.

Depth profile — an analyte against depth, one trace per pit, logged horizon boundaries as breaks and the composite intervals as bands. The depth axis is the one thing this matrix has that water samples do not, and a table of intervals is the least legible way to show that the signal sits in the second and third horizons rather than at the surface. It is a figure family outside the twelve approved renderings — a depth-down vertical axis, and banded intervals rather than points or a line, are moves none of them makes. What it needs first: A written grammar proposal to Jerry, on the screen that would use it, in the same shape as the Piper/Stiff/Durov proposals the catalogue already defers. Recorded here rather than left out, because a reader arriving at a depth-intervalled investigation will look for the plate and is owed the reason it is absent. And the standing caveat would attach to it as it attaches to every plate here: the grammar has never been print-tested (G-76b).

An amendment on a round that has already been reported

PAS2026-01884 rev B re-reports 3 results on 2026-Q1-GW, and that round is inside a locked period.

The period 2025 Q1 – 2026 Q1 — locked, reported to DWER was closed to writes when the 2026 Q1 report went to DWER, and a locked period refuses a write rather than warning about one. The amended values are staged: computed, previewed, and standing nowhere. Nothing on the exceedance register, the TARP board or the licence has moved, and nothing will until somebody decides. What follows is what accepting would do.

Why the laboratory re-issued

Finding 1 — Calibration blank contamination — dissolved metals, ICP-MS run of 2026-02-10

The laboratory’s own quarterly review of its calibration records found the blank used to standardise positions 7 to 12 of batch PAS-WO-261188 carried copper and zinc above its acceptance limit. Copper and zinc on the samples in those positions were reported high. Nickel, cadmium and the major cations were unaffected — they were not in the contaminated blank.

Re-analysed on 2026-07-28 from the retained, acid-preserved aliquots. The samples were collected on 2026-02-04, so the re-analysis sits inside the six-month holding time for dissolved metals, which closes on 2026-08-04. Outside that window the amendment would not have been analytically defensible and the laboratory says so on the certificate.

Finding 2 — Dilution factor — EDTA hardness titration, same batch

The titration was performed at a 1-in-5 dilution, recorded as such on the bench sheet, and reported against a 1-in-4 factor. The reported hardness is 25% low.

No re-analysis: the titration reading is on the bench sheet and only the factor applied to it was wrong, so the correction is arithmetic and exact — 268 × 1.25 = 335 mg/L as CaCO₃.

On the numbering: Pilbara Analytical Services numbers a whole re-issue afresh and suffixes a partial one: PAS2026-04398 became PAS2026-04417 because every result on it was re-reported, and this one keeps its reference with a revision because three results on it did. Which document stands is a supersession either way.

  2. 2

Against the issued hardness that is −20.6%, outside the ±10% limit; against the amended one, −0.8%.

What the withdrawn trip reaches

Copper at MW05 tripped on 2026-Q1-GW, and that trip is what raised the groundwater investigation programme lodged with DWER on 2026-02-27. Accepting the amendment does not un-lodge it: a document that has gone to a regulator is withdrawn by writing to the regulator, and the product records which of those happened rather than doing the second one.

The 2026 Q2 exceedance register would also read differently. Copper at MW05 would read first rather than 4th consecutive quarter, and zinc first rather than 2nd consecutive quarter — the run column is counted from the rounds, so it moves when a round does.

The window and the criterion in force at each round are frozen onto the outcome. A licence varied next year re-evaluates future rounds and moves nothing already decided — the same rule the notification screen keeps about a deadline.

The two series that do not move, and why not

●holds Zinc (filtered) at MW07 — MW07 was analysed in a different position on the run and is not covered by either finding. Its values do not move, so its run does not.

●holds Electrical conductivity at MW05 — Electrical conductivity is read on a conductivity cell, not out of the metals digest. Neither finding reaches it.

Stating why a series did not change is the half of an impact preview that is usually left out, and it is the half a reader needs in order to trust the half that did.

The decision

Accept the amendment into a locked period, record it as no material impact, or hold it and ask the laboratory.

Accepting the amendment into a locked period would write:

  • Supersessions appended, with a reason on each3
  • Results whose value is replaced in place0 — a superseded value stays readable
  • Assessed outcomes recomputed4
  • Outcomes that change2
  • Windowed series re-evaluated4, of which 2 change
  • Licence conditions whose outcome moves1 — 12(c), from triggered to not triggered
  • Obligations already lodged that this puts in question1
  • Issued documents altered0 — a snapshot is what was issued
  • Snapshots flagged for reissue review1
  • 2026 Q2 results touched0

Accepting appends supersessions, and an appended supersession is never deleted. A decision made in error is corrected by a further supersession that names what it corrects, and both stay readable. What is reversible is the evaluation rather than the record: outcomes are recomputed from the values that stand, so a correction moves them back.

The ways out, each with what it writes

Three options and a refusal. None of them deletes anything, and none is the default (PP4, QB-7).
OptionWhat it does
Accept the amendmentWrites 3 supersessions against a locked period with the reason on each, re-evaluates 2026-Q1-GW, withdraws 2 exceedances, recomputes 2 window runs, withdraws the condition 12(c) trip, and flags snapshot SNAP-0117 and the 2026 Q2 draft as stale. It does not delete anything and it does not reissue anything: the reissue is its own decision, on its own screen.
Record as no material impactWrites a decision record with a stated reason and leaves the standing values where they are. The amended certificate stays attached to the round and findable. A blank reason is refused — “no impact” with nothing behind it is the judgement this record exists to hold.
Hold, and ask the laboratoryWrites a query against the certificate and nothing else. The amendment stays staged and the round stays locked. Use it where the re-analysis itself is in question rather than the arithmetic.

What is refused, and what cannot be undone

Refused: Replacing the three values in place. The period is locked because it has been reported to DWER, and a locked period refuses the write rather than warning about it — a number that has gone to a regulator is superseded with a reason or it is not changed.

Irreversible: Accepting appends supersessions, and an appended supersession is never deleted. A decision made in error is corrected by a further supersession that names what it corrects, and both stay readable. What is reversible is the evaluation rather than the record: outcomes are recomputed from the values that stand, so a correction moves them back.

Validation state and qualifiers came across, not just numbers.

FR-3.11 asks for the historical validation state to survive the move. A migration that lands the values and drops twenty years of qualifiers has moved the data and lost the record.

The same proof, read at the other end

A migration proves what arrived: source rows against loaded rows, source exceedances against evaluated ones, and a count that disagrees is a migration nobody should trust. An export owes the mirror of it — a file leaving this instance is somebody else’s source, and it is trusted on exactly the same evidence. One discipline, read twice.

Read twice, it is not symmetrical, and that is the finding rather than a gap in the drawing. The table above agrees on every row it can compute. The 2026 Q2 export’s reconciliation runs 10 checks and 5 agree; the other 5 cannot, because what this instance holds has nowhere to land in the target format. An import can be complete. An export into somebody else’s vocabulary can only be honest about what it dropped.

Every format that crosses the boundary

The direction that is proved is the direction that was built.

FR-3.11 asks for a reconciliation on the way in and this screen is it. FR-7.6 asks for regulator-format and EQuIS-compatible output on the way out, and the requirement is marked S8 — so the mirror is drawn as a proposal rather than claimed, and the 2 outbound formats sit beside the 5 inbound ones so the imbalance is visible instead of implied.

Exchange formats

Every format that crosses this instance’s boundary, in either direction — what each one preserves, and what it cannot carry.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. Five screens describe formats coming in and none of them answers what leaves, or on whose terms.

Import runs owns the runs, EDD formats a laboratory’s file shape, Mapping profiles what the importer learned from each laboratory, Legacy reconciliation one historical move, Held rows what a format could not resolve. All five look one way. The decision this screen exists for is taken before a file is written and cannot be taken on any of them: this deliverable is owed under a contract, in a vocabulary that is not ours — what survives the crossing, and what does the receiving system read where something does not? FR-7.6 is marked S8 in the product’s own sequencing and drawing it here does not reschedule it.

What crosses the boundary

A format is a durable record with an owner and a version, and the two things worth knowing about one are not its field count. They are what it preserves and what it cannot carry — and the second is the column no format registry ever has, which is why a loss is usually discovered by the person receiving the file rather than by the person writing it.

7 formats — 5 inbound, 2 outbound. 4 of them have read a real file on this project; the rest are defined and unexercised, and the column says which.

This register restates none of those screens. It holds the two facts none of them carries — which way the file goes, and what the crossing costs — and the second is the table below.

A PQL — the format carries four limits and none of them is verified as one. A field duplicate, a field blank or an equipment blank — there is no code for any of the three, and a blind duplicate reaches a laboratory as Normal.

What is not on this list. The four shapes every Export ▾ menu writes — workbook, CSV, Word table, vector figure — are this product’s own output in general-purpose containers, conforming to nobody’s specification and translating nothing. A format is on this register when somebody else owns its vocabulary, which is what creates a mapping and therefore a loss. The customer’s report template is owned by somebody else and is still not here: it carries prose and figures rather than records, so nothing in it is renamed on the way out.

5 in, 2 out — and only one of the 2 is a file this instance writes.

The other is a form somebody fills in on a regulator’s portal. That imbalance is not an oversight in the drawing; it is what a system of record for one jurisdiction looks like when the jurisdiction takes its returns by hand. It is also why the single file below is drawn in depth rather than the register being drawn in breadth: parity with EQuIS across its full breadth is a stated non-goal, and a format zoo would be the wrong answer to a contractual clause.
