Subterranean fauna

The receptor downgradient of the TSF, assessed on whether a population persists.

/projects/:projectId/fauna

These results are not chemistry, and forcing them into a concentration model would lose them.

A stygofauna survey produces counts of taxa against a reference site, on a net-haul method, assessed for whether a population persists — not a value against a limit. The EPA conditions mining approvals in this state on exactly this, and a groundwater platform for WA mining with nowhere to put it is visibly not built for WA.

Condition
Ministerial statement 1184 condition 9 — subterranean fauna monitoring
Method
Net haul, 150 µm and 50 µm, three hauls per bore per event · EPA Technical Guidance, subterranean fauna survey
Frequency
Twice yearly — one wet season, one dry
Reference bore
STY01
Downgradient bore
STY02
Survey events, reference against downgradient.
BoreRoleEventTaxaIndividualsNotableVerdict
STY01Reference2026 dry741Bathynellidae sp. B04 — short-range endemic●persisting
STY02Downgradient2026 dry412Bathynellidae sp. B04 — 2 individuals◐reduced against reference
STY01Reference2025 wet855Bathynellidae sp. B04, Candonidae sp. C11●persisting
STY02Downgradient2025 wet628Bathynellidae sp. B04 — 9 individuals●persisting

What it appears to say

Taxa richness at STY02 has fallen from 6 to 4 and individual counts from 28 to 12 across two events, while the reference bore held steady. The salinity and sulfate rise at MW05 sits between the two. This is the receptor the water-quality exceedances are ultimately about, and it is assessed on population persistence rather than against a concentration.

Two bores, two events

Taxa richness at the downgradient bore has fallen while the reference held steady, and the salinity and sulfate rise at MW05 sits geographically between them. That is a coherent story and it is not yet evidence.

Background comparisonFlow direction

And why the product will not draw a trend through it

Two events is not a trend. Stygofauna counts vary by an order of magnitude with season, haul effort and operator, and the honest reading is that this warrants a targeted survey rather than a conclusion. The screen says so rather than drawing a line through two points.

Everywhere else in this product a series of numbers gets a trend test. Here it does not, and the refusal is the design: counts that vary by an order of magnitude with season, haul effort and operator do not support one, and a Mann–Kendall drawn across four points would look exactly as authoritative as the arsenic plate that is built on fourteen.

◐ Two events. A trend needs more, and the product says so instead of drawing one.

The screen states what changed and recommends a targeted survey. It does not compute a rate, because a rate here would be a number with a confidence interval that nothing in the sampling design supports — and it would be quoted back for years.

Map

The monitoring network, symbolised by this round’s outcome.

/projects/:projectId/map

Which way the water goes

Every location on this project carries a position — upgradient, downgradient of TSF, compliance boundary — and until this plate those were attributes somebody typed. This derives them.

The surface is a planar least-squares fit through the 7 superficial bores that carry a head this round. That is the honest method for a network this size: it states one gradient and one direction and cannot invent local structure the data does not support. Interpolating a curved surface through seven bores draws detail nobody measured, and it is the picture that gets argued with.

MW11 is drawn and is not a control point. It was dipped to the base of its screened interval on 14 May and found dry, so it has no standing level and therefore no head — it had been contributing one, a water table fifteen metres above where the tape found nothing. The bore stays on the plate with an open mark and the word: a compliance-boundary bore that disappears from a network map because it held no water that week is the reading this figure can least afford.

The network geometry decides whether this figure is possible at all. Six of these bores sit almost on one line, and a plane fitted through collinear points is barely constrained across that line — the first version of this plate returned a flow direction of due south on a site whose every other screen says south-east, with a residual of 1.46 m against its own one-metre limit. Two bores genuinely off the transect fixed it. That is why the residual is printed on the plate rather than kept in a log: it is the figure telling you whether to believe it.

MW03B is excluded. It screens the confined unit. Contouring two aquifers as one surface is the commonest error on a plate like this, and it produces a flow direction that is an average of two systems and true of neither.

What it confirms

Flow runs from the north-west to the east-south-east — 119° at 1.93 m/km, on a largest residual of 0.04 m — so a planar surface fits this network almost exactly. The TSF sits upgradient of MW05 and MW07, which sit upgradient of the compliance boundary at MW09 and MW11. The stored positions are correct — and these three numbers are read off the fit rather than typed beside it, which is what let removing a phantom head move them without leaving a stale sentence behind.

Symbology

Worst outcome per location across every criteria set. A bore compliant against the licence and above an ANZG guideline value reads as an exceedance, because that is the more consequential of the two.

Shape, not colour. The print layout is the same map at A3 with a north arrow, a bar scale, a grid and a title block — and it survives a monochrome office printer, which is where most of them end up.

Spatial export

ShapefileLocations, state, latest resultGDA2020 / MGA zone 50 (EPSG:7850)

GDA2020 is not WGS84. They agree only at epoch 2020.0 and separate by about 7 cm a year, so a WGS84 export carries its epoch and a conversion without one is refused rather than assumed.

Template and numbering

Reference

A failing comparison blocks the snapshot, not the draft. Writing continues; issuing does not — which is the only point in the loop where the check is worth anything.

What a comparison is for

Every other check in this product measures the document against a rule — a unit is present, a reference resolves. This one measures it against an approved copy, which is the only way to catch a change nobody thought to write a rule about.

The reference is an oracle: it is approved once, by a person, and the assembled document is compared to it. Changing the reference and the document that asserts against it in the same act would make the comparison agree with itself, which is the failure mode of every golden test ever written in a hurry.

One row per check. What the reference expects, what the assembled document carries, and whether they agree.

Both failures are the same failure: the prescribed form requires an authored section and the document has 0 words in §6 and 0 words in §7. Nothing is wrong with the generated content — the crosstab, the registers and the figures all match the reference. The report is a draft, and the gate is saying so at the one moment it is worth saying: the moment somebody tries to issue it.

Write §6What a snapshot would captureWriting continues either way. Only issuing is blocked.

What a failure that is not an unfinished draft looks like — 2026-08-19 16:40 AWST

§3.2 — QA/QC summary table. The golden reference carries seven columns and the assembled table carried six: Action taken was dropped when the QA/QC generator changed.

Nothing in the document looked wrong. Every check that reads the document’s own structure passed, and a reader who had never seen the reference would have found §3.2 unremarkable — which is exactly why the comparison is against an approved copy rather than against a rule.

The generator was corrected and §3.2 regenerated the same afternoon. The failing run is kept; a gate with no record of what it caught is indistinguishable from one that has never fired.

Two items are stale, and each says what made it stale

Figure 5.1 Condition 12(c) — four rounds, four series — the staged amendment reaches two of its four series.

Table 5.1 Exceedance register — MW03B superseded.

Table 5.1 was generated before the laboratory amended PAS2026-04398: arsenic at MW03B went from 31 to 3.1 and stopped being an exceedance. Figure 5.1 draws the four rounds of condition 12(c), two of whose series the staged amendment reaches.

Both are marked stale rather than silently regenerated. A figure that changes underneath a paragraph somebody has already written is how a report comes to contradict itself — and one of these two would change on a decision nobody has taken yet.

Stale is not the same as changed. Figure 6.1 is current on this register and does not appear above: it regenerated cleanly when MW11 stopped contributing a head. What that regeneration reached is a sentence in §6.1 that cites it, and the flag sits there, against the passage, rather than here against the plate. A figure being out of date and a figure having changed under an author are two findings and they belong on two screens.

Decide the amendment first

A number this document does not carry

Every cross-reference is checked against the numbers the document actually carries, and 18 of them resolve. A reference to Figure 4.9 would not: §4 carries 6 figures, and a reference past the end of a section is a finding rather than a rendering that quietly prints the literal text.

This is the check that costs nothing and that nobody runs. A dangling cross-reference survives every proofread, because the sentence around it reads perfectly well.

Inserting a figure, and what it renumbers

Adding Copper at MW05 across four rounds after Figure 4.2 makes it Figure 4.3. The copper series is what the staged amendment turns on, and §5.3 asserts a trip that a reader cannot check without seeing four rounds beside each other.

2 references in authored prose, and neither of them breaks — which is a change this wave made rather than a claim it inherited.

§6 Interpretation refers to Figure 4.3 and Figure 4.6. Until wave 7 those were numbers typed into sentences a hydrogeologist wrote, the insert would have made both wrong, and the product’s answer was to raise them as findings and refuse to edit the prose. They are cross-reference tokens now: the sentence refers to the item, the number is rendered from wherever the item sits, and the insert moves both renderings without touching a word or raising anything. The prose is still never rewritten — there is simply nothing left in it to rewrite. What still flags a sentence is the referenced figure’s content changing, and one of §6’s four tokens is flagged for exactly that today.

Interpretation — §6

Where the hydrogeologist writes, with the evidence for the claim beside them.

a proposal — not in the product

Proposed. FR-7 generates a report but nothing authors one.

FR-7.1 to FR-7.6 cover templates, numbering, snapshots and branding — the mechanics of assembly. A monitoring report is roughly half interpretive prose, and nothing in the requirement set says where that prose is written. Today the answer is Word, which reintroduces exactly the round trip QB-2 exists to remove.

The rule this workspace applies to every number in a sentence: Three significant figures, and never more than the source publishes.

A number quoted in a sentence renders to the precision its source publishes, capped at three significant figures. A citation is checked under this rule: the question is whether the rendered form moved, not whether the stored value did. Without it, a stored value that gains digits — a statistics worker returning four decimal places where it returned two — flags a sentence that has not become wrong. The author then learns that the flag means nothing, which is the failure mode of every staleness indicator that cries wolf. It governs prose only. A statistics table and a plate carry the precision of the analysis, and 1.77 in a table beside 1.77 in a sentence is the rule agreeing with itself rather than two surfaces disagreeing.

6.1 Groundwater quality at MW05

A. Nakamura · 2026-08-24 08:51 AWST

Arsenic at MW05 was reported at 28.4 µg/L — cited value, agreeing with its source, above the ANZG 2018 95% species protection guideline value of 13 µg/L — cited value, agreeing with its source and the third consecutive quarter above that value §Figure 4.2 — cross-reference token to “Arsenic at MW05, with censoring”.

Mann–Kendall over fourteen quarterly rounds reports a significant increasing trend (0.003 — cited value, agreeing with its source) with a Sen’s slope of 1.77 µg/L per quarter — cited value, agreeing: the source moved to 1.7666666666666666 and renders unchanged under the rendering rule §Figure 4.6 — cross-reference token to “Arsenic trend at MW05”.

The major-ion signature at MW05 is sulfate-dominated and distinct from the calcium–bicarbonate background of every other bore §Figure 4.3 — cross-reference token to “Piper trilinear diagram”; the bore sits directly downgradient of the tailings storage facility on the May 2026 potentiometric surface §Figure 6.1▲ changed — cross-reference token to “Potentiometric surface, May 2026”, flagged because the referenced figure’s content changed; and every elevated parameter is elevated against the site’s own background as well as against a guideline value. Taken together this is consistent with seepage from the tailings storage facility rather than with natural variation.

Cadmium could not be assessed at any location this round: the laboratory’s limit of reporting of 1.0 µg/L sits above the guideline value of 0.54 µg/L

The evidence set, pinned to the sentence

§6.1, third paragraph — the seepage inference. Pinned by A. Nakamura · 2026-08-24 09:12 AWST · 8 items, 7 of them drawn on this project.

Pinned to the sentence, kept with it, and shown to whoever reviews it. This is what the author had in front of them when they wrote it.

The panel beside the editor answers are my citations numerically correct. This one answers the harder question — does the evidence support what I am claiming — and it answers it by showing the evidence, not by judging it. There is no score here, no confidence, no strength, and no count of evidence for against evidence against. Every tile says what it shows and what it does not settle, because the second is what keeps a set of evidence from becoming a set of arguments. Each opens the plate or the record at full size: a Piper diagram drawn to 180 mm is a grey triangle at tile width, so the tile is a reference rather than a thumbnail.

Hydrograph

●drawn on this project

Figure 4.1 — groundwater elevation at MW05, MW07 and MW01A, with rainfall

Shows: A falling trend at MW05 through three years of wet-season recovery, against two bores that hold level. The seepage mound is a water-level story before it is a chemistry one.

Does not settle: A hydrograph cannot distinguish seepage from abstraction. There is no production bore within 400 m of MW05, and that is a fact off the location register rather than something this plate shows.

Open it at full size

Head contours

●drawn on this project

Figure 6.1 — potentiometric surface and flow direction, May 2026

Shows: A planar least-squares fit through the superficial bores that carry a head this round, with the largest residual printed on the plate. It puts the tailings storage facility upgradient of MW05 and MW07, and those upgradient of the compliance boundary.

Does not settle: A plane states one gradient and one direction. It cannot show local structure, and it says nothing about vertical flow — that argument is the nest at MW01A/MW03B, which is its own record.

Open it at full size

Major-ion signature

●drawn on this project

Figure 4.3 — Piper trilinear diagram, and Figure 4.4 — Stiff diagrams by location

Shows: MW05 plots away from every other bore on the sulfate limb while the background and upgradient bores cluster as calcium–bicarbonate waters. A signature, not a concentration.

Does not settle: A distinct signature says this water is different. It does not say what made it different, and evaporative concentration would move a bore along the same limb.

Source chemistry

◐not held — stated, not filled

No analysis of the tailings liquor is held on this project

Shows: Nothing. The only TSF record here is the embankment piezometer TSF-VWP-03, which measures a phreatic surface and not a chemistry.

Does not settle: This is the piece of evidence that would settle it, and it is absent. The inference rests on the pattern at MW05 against the site’s own background rather than on a source fingerprint, and the reviewer is told that here rather than discovering it.

Owed: A decant or underdrainage analysis would make the comparison direct. It is a sampling decision, not a software one.

Does not settle: A background comparison establishes difference from the reference population. Attribution to a particular source is the hydrogeologist’s inference, and this screen is one of its inputs.

Bore construction

●drawn on this project

MW05 construction log — screened interval, casing, annulus and the survey the datum stands on

Shows: The screen sits wholly within the weathered granite below a bentonite seal, so the sample represents the superficial aquifer at 12–18 m and nothing above it. uPVC casing throughout, which is why a metals result here is not read against a steel-cased bore.

Does not settle: Construction says what the sample represents. It cannot say whether the water reaching that interval came from the tailings storage facility.

The one piece of evidence this project does not hold

Of the 8 items on the list, 1 has nothing behind it: Source chemistry. No analysis of the tailings liquor exists on this project, and it is the one comparison that would make the inference direct rather than circumstantial.

It is drawn as the gap it is. An evidence set that quietly omitted the evidence nobody has would let a reviewer assume it had been considered and found consistent — which is the opposite of what happened.

A decant or underdrainage analysis would make the comparison direct. It is a sampling decision, not a software one.

No new figure family was drawn for any of this. The head-contour tile references the potentiometric plate the catalogue already has; the grammar is frozen and a new family is a written proposal to Jerry before it is a rendering.

The competing explanations, in the author’s own words

A reviewer asking did you consider the alternatives should not have to ask. These are recorded with the passage and attributed, and they are authored content — a product that proposed the alternatives would be proposing the conclusion.

AlternativeWhat the author recorded
Evaporative concentration in a shallow boreA. NakamuraWould move the bore along the sulfate limb and raise every ion together. Chloride has not moved with sulfate here, and the ratio is the test.
Natural sulfate from the weathered profileA. NakamuraMW12 and MW01A are screened in the same unit and show none of it, which is what makes the background comparison the load-bearing evidence rather than a formality.
Abstraction drawing older, more mineralised waterA. NakamuraNo production bore within 400 m, and the hydrograph shows a decline that does not follow the borefield’s pumping pattern.
A laboratory or sampling artefactA. NakamuraFour consecutive rounds, two laboratories on the PFAS suite, and the field and equipment blanks clear. A four-round artefact is a different and larger claim than a seepage one.

Refused: The product does not weigh these against each other and does not tell the author which one is right. It keeps them with the sentence so a reviewer can see that they were considered, and so a reviewer who disagrees knows exactly what to disagree with.

Not flagged — the value gained digits and the sentence did not change

Sen’s slope. The sentence was written when the source published 1.77. It publishes 1.7666666666666666 now. The stats worker returns the slope at full precision since the 2026-08-19 upgrade; it returned two decimal places before. Nothing about the series changed and nothing about the finding changed — the number simply arrived with more digits on it.

Under the rule both render 1.77, so the sentence says exactly what it said and it is not flagged. This is the case the review named: 1.7 against 1.72 is formatting, and a workspace that flagged it would teach the author that flags mean nothing.

It governs prose only. A statistics table and a plate carry the precision of the analysis, and 1.77 in a table beside 1.77 in a sentence is the rule agreeing with itself rather than two surfaces disagreeing.

Flagged — the value moved, and so did the outcome it carried

Arsenic at MW03B. The §6.2 sentence was written on 31 µg/L. The laboratory re-issued the certificate: Laboratory re-issued the certificate — transcription error at the laboratory, decimal point. The record now says 3.1 µg/L, and compliant against ANZG 2018.

So the sentence is wrong, and it stays on the screen exactly as its author wrote it. The workspace names it, shows both values, and offers the correction — taking it is the author’s act, attributed to them like any other write.

What the re-issue changed

A product that had silently rewritten this would have produced a report whose §6.2 nobody had read, standing on a value nobody had checked.

A number that changed, and a diagram that changed

Renumbering does not flag a sentence

The Piper reference in §6.1 is a cross-reference token, not the characters Figure 4.3 typed into the prose. It resolves to the item and renders whatever number that item carries.

TokenRenders nowUnder the staged insertSentence
Trend plotFigure 4.6Figure 4.7●not flagged
Piper diagramFigure 4.3Figure 4.4●not flagged

Inserting a figure after Figure 4.2 renumbers 2 of the items §6.1 cites. Both tokens would silently render their new numbers, and neither sentence is flagged, because neither sentence ever contained a number.

This is the distinction the review asked for. Renumbering is a fact about the document’s ordering; it tells an author nothing and asking them to re-read four sentences for it is how a flag becomes noise.

A diagram that changed does flag it

The same sentence cites Figure 6.1▲ changed — the potentiometric surface. Its number has not moved. Its content has.

MW11 was dipped to the base of its screened interval on 14 May and found dry, so it carries no head and is no longer a control point on the fit. The plate is fitted through seven bores where it was fitted through eight, and it draws MW11 as a dry bore rather than omitting it.

What moved: The flow direction and the gradient both moved, in the third significant figure. The reading the sentence makes — the TSF sits upgradient of MW05 — did not. The fit now runs through 7 bores rather than 8: flow 119° at 1.93 m/km, largest residual 0.04 m.

What is owed: The author is asked to look at the plate and confirm the sentence still says what they meant. Nothing about the sentence has been changed, and nothing will be.

Open the plate as it stands nowWhy MW11 carries no head

Four things this workspace will not do, drawn as refusals rather than left unimplemented.

  • Rewrite a flagged sentence with the current value. A sentence somebody wrote is theirs. The workspace names it, shows both values and offers the correction; taking it is the author’s act and it is attributed to them.
  • Score the inference, or rate the evidence. The evidence set exists so a reviewer sees what the author saw. A product that graded a hydrogeological judgement would be making one, in somebody else’s name.
  • Flag a sentence because a figure was renumbered. The sentence never contained the number. A cross-reference token resolves to the item, so renumbering moves the rendering and leaves the prose alone.
  • Flag a sentence because a stored value gained digits. The rendering rule decides what the sentence says. If the rendered form has not moved, nothing a reader can see has changed.

7 differences across 4 sections, from 3 amended results — which is the ratio worth noticing. Three numbers move and seven things in the document change, because a monitoring report says the same result in several places and each of them is a place a hand-edit misses.

The issued artifact is immutable, and that is not the same claim as “nothing has changed”.

The bytes lodged with DWER on 2026-04-28 are held and reproducible; no amendment, no re-evaluation and no configuration change reaches them. What can change is the record they were drawn from, and the two columns above keep those apart so that “what did you report” and “what do you now believe” are separately answerable years later.

Reissuing

Reissuing the 2026 Q1 report would write:

  • New snapshot taken1 — SNAP-0124, with its own digest
  • Results it would stand on228 — 3 at amended values
  • Sign-offs required again3 — prepared, reviewed, approved
  • The issued document SNAP-01170 changes — it is what was lodged and stays so
  • Submission record1 new · the accepted 2026 Q1 submission is superseded, not replaced
  • Sections needing an author before it can go1 — §6.1 cites a trip that would no longer stand

A reissue is reversible up to lodgement and not after: the new snapshot can be discarded while it is a draft, and a document that has gone to DWER is withdrawn by writing to DWER. The product records which of those happened; it cannot do the second one for you.

Not available while the amendment is staged. A reissue that regenerated against values nobody has accepted would put an undecided number into a regulatory submission. The control is drawn and refuses, rather than being absent: somebody deciding the amendment upstairs needs to see what a reissue costs before they decide, not after.

The same register, taken apart

Every aggregate above is decomposable, and it is decomposed here rather than left as a number somebody has to trust. The two rows add to the four tiles.

Following a MOCK-KRJ row is a scope switch and not a link: the header, the section strip and what every other screen is about all change with it. This catalogue draws one of the two workspaces, so the switch is where it stops — which is stated here rather than discovered by clicking.

Four kinds of clock on one board, counted

They compete for the same week, which is why they share a register — but they are not the same obligation and the difference decides what missing one costs.

KindRowsWhat starts the clock
Reporting obligation6A cadence a licence condition sets — the wording survives, and interpreting it into a date comes later
Programme round5A period ending. Written when the period ends rather than when somebody looks, which is what makes a missed one nameable
Notification obligation2An event. The window is short enough that missing it is the incident — and where the condition says as soon as practicable, no number of hours is invented
Trigger response2A criterion being crossed. The deadline is arithmetic on the evaluation date, so it can run without a person being involved at any point

The MOCK-KRJ row is the last kind: the operating strategy gives thirty days from evaluation, so its deadline is 2025-11-06 plus thirty and nothing anybody typed — which is also how it reached overdue by 169 days with no person in the loop.

A monitoring period is resolved in the site’s own timezone, never the server’s.

A quarterly round at a Pilbara bore begins at 16:00 UTC on 31 December. A sample collected at 08:00 on 1 April local time belongs to the June quarter — get it wrong and the round it was meant to satisfy reads as missed while a spurious extra one reads as satisfied. Both projects on this register resolve in Australia/Perth; a register spanning two zones would resolve each row in its own site’s, never in one chosen for the board.

MW05 is on two programmes, and a screen showing one of them would be wrong.

GW-QTR runs quarterly across the network. GW-MTH runs monthly at MW05 and MW07, and has since 2026-03-01, because a TARP Level 2 trigger required increased frequency — so MW05 is next due on 2026-06-14, not 2026-08-14. A programme that read as satisfied while a monthly round went uncollected is the two-surfaces-disagree failure this product exists to end, and it is the escalated round that gets missed because it is the one nobody planned for.

A frequency raised by a trigger comes back down by a decision

GW-MTH exists because the data crossed a line, and it does not lapse when the data recrosses it. Standing it down is a decision somebody makes and signs, against the TARP’s own stand-down condition — four consecutive rounds below the trigger — because a monitoring frequency that relaxed itself the first quiet quarter is the one that misses the next event.

Standing GW-MTH down would:

  • Rounds removed from the calendar8 per year
  • Consecutive rounds below trigger required4 — currently 0
  • TARP level this would return MW05 toLevel 1
  • Historical rounds affected0

The control is present and refuses, rather than absent. An operator who cannot see what would release them from a monitoring burden cannot plan against it.

Water take against entitlement

▲ Approaching the entitlement — projected 1,164.3 ML at 30 September, 93.1% of 1,250.0 ML.

The flag trips at 90% projected, and the projection is the mean of the 7 complete months — 97.0 ML a month — over twelve. It is a warning about a return, not a breach: 570.8 ML of the entitlement is unused, the 5 months left may average 114.2 ML, and the year to date has averaged 97.0 ML. Nothing is owed because of this flag, and that is deliberate — the obligation is the annual water return, which falls due whatever the number is.

The year runs from the anniversary of the water licence’s grant — 1 October 2019 — because that is what the instrument says. A July boundary here would be the WA fiscal year borrowed out of habit, and it would put four months of this year’s take into last year’s return.

A year is named by the month it ends, so the 2026 entitlement year began on 1 October 2025. The boundary is 00:00 on 1 October at the site, which is 16:00 UTC on 30 September. A volume logged at 07:00 AWST on 1 October belongs to the year beginning, never to the year ending — resolved in Australia/Perth, never on the server.

Four calendar quarters tile this year exactly, which is why the quarterly discharge returns sit inside it without splitting. The groundwater monitoring year does not: it ends in June and cuts this one in half.

The running position

679.2 of 1,250.0 ML taken54%

54.3% of the entitlement against 58.1% of the year elapsed — 212 of 365 days. The comparison is the point: a volume without its share of the year is a number nobody can act on.

The comparison is made in kilolitres, not megalitres. 679,190 kL is 679.2 ML displayed, and the entitlement is a legal limit — a rounding that lands a kilolitre over it would be an exceedance nobody caused.

May is a meter totaliser read on the 23rd, not an extraction record: an extraction record is a reported volume for a period that has ended. It is shown because a practitioner asks, and it is in no rate on this page.

≈ marks a volume that was estimated rather than metered, so the basis reads across the row without reading the notes; on the totals row it marks a month that contains one. There is no third basis: a volume was measured by a meter or it was estimated, and a return that presented the two alike would overstate its own reliability.

The two volumes nobody metered

◐estimated PB02 · Feb 2026 — 44.3 ML from 412 pump run hours × 107.5 kL/h. The meter was out of service for 23 days of the month. The duty rate is the one MF-2212 itself measured in January and the hours come from the pump controller, so neither input is an assumption about this bore.

◐estimated PB03 · Oct 2025 — 26.0 ML from 200 pump run hours × 130 kL/h. No meter was ever fitted to PB03. The rate is its last capacity test, in 2021, which is the weakest evidence on this page — so it is marked wherever the volume appears rather than only here.

Together they are 70.3 ML — 10.3% of the take on the record. The total above carries them because the entitlement counts every kilolitre however it was measured; what changes is the confidence, and that is printed rather than absorbed.

PB03 has no meter at all and was decommissioned on 2025-11-04, inside this year. A bore that no longer exists still took water in October, and dropping the row would make the year’s total smaller than the year’s take.

What the projection rests on

Three defensible rules over the same volumes, and only one of them is in force.
RuleWhat the rate is overProjectedAgainst the flag
Complete months, every borein force7 months Oct – Apr · 3 bores1,164.3 ML · 93.1%■over 90%
Counting May as a month8 months Oct – May · 3 bores1,115.4 ML · 89.2%○under 90%
Operating bores only7 months Oct – Apr · 2 bores1,119.8 ML · 89.6%○under 90%

A part month divided as though it were a whole one understates the rate by a fifth. And the rate in force runs 26.0 ML of PB03’s October take forward for five more months, through a bore that was decommissioned on 2025-11-04 — on the 2 bores still operating the rate is 93.3 ML a month rather than 97.0.

So the position is marginal, and the flag says so rather than reading as a forecast. 93.1% against a 90% threshold, with two defensible variations of the rule landing under it. Neither variation is applied here: which months and which bores a projection runs over is a rule, and a rule that decides a flag has to be configured and versioned before it is used, never chosen because it gives the quieter answer.

Recording May’s volume — refused, and why

The obvious next act on this screen is to enter the number the meter is showing. It is refused, because the period it would be recorded against has not ended.

Recording 64.4 ML against May today would:

  • Take on the record679.2 → 743.6 ML
  • Months in the rate7 → 8
  • Projection at year end1,164.3 → 1,115.4 ML
  • The approaching-limit flag93.1% → 89.2% — the flag clears
  • Water actually taken0 ML difference

The last two rows are the whole argument: the flag would clear without a litre less being taken, because a fuller-looking record changes what the rate is computed over. An extraction record is a reported volume for a period that has ended — and once the annual return is lodged the period is locked, so a wrong volume is corrected by supersession rather than edited.

Refused: recording a totaliser reading as the month’s volume while the month is running. There is no control for it, rather than a control that warns — the reading is real and it is on the page above, and what it is not is a record of a period.

Volume metered at discharge point DP01, concentration sampled at SW01 — the point the licence names for it, 200 m downstream. The load is therefore reported at the compliance point rather than at the outfall; moving the sample is a licence variation, not a setting on this screen.

concentration × volume ÷ 1000 — mg/L × kL gives kilograms, µg/L × kL gives grams. One grab sample per quarter, against the quarter’s metered volume.

A censored concentration is a decision, not a number

Copper was below the limit of reporting in 2 of the 3 quarters. Nothing was measured, so no load can be computed — and a total that goes to a regulator is the last place to substitute a number nobody read. The quarter carries the interval its two bounding substitutions give, and the four treatments sit beside it.

Copper at SW01, 2025 Q4 — 14,300 kL at < 0.5 µg/L, under each treatment.
TreatmentLoadWhat it asserts
excludebound to the criteria set todayno loadThe quarter has no reportable load — which is not the same as a quarter that discharged nothing.
zero0.0 gThat no copper left the site. Nothing measured says that.
half the LOR3.6 gA number nobody read, printed to one decimal. FR-5.8 refuses it as a default.
the LOR7.2 gThe most that could have been there — the upper bound, and true as one.

The criteria set in force binds exclude, and that binding is not inherited here: evaluation asks whether one value is above a limit, and a load asks what total to report. The load is drawn as the interval — 0.0 – 7.2 g — with both bounds named. The treatments the criteria set can bind are the same four.

The year’s load, and what it does not claim

AnalyteEntitlement year to dateBasis
Nitrate as N286.4 kgDetected in every quarter
Copper (filtered)94.1 – 103.6 gBounded — two quarters censored

One grab sample against three months of volume is a first-order load, and the screen says so rather than printing three significant figures at it. A flow-weighted composite would answer better; the licence asks for a grab, and the number that goes into the return is the one the licence asks for.

October discharged nothing at all. A zero volume is not a missing reading and the row says which it is — a month with no discharge contributes no load, and a month nobody read would contribute an unknown one.

What exceeding the entitlement would oblige

Condition 23 of L8842/2019/1 restates the same volume, so taking more than the entitlement breaches two instruments at once — the water licence the entitlement belongs to, and the environmental licence that mirrors it.

  1. 1The take passes the entitlementMeasured in kilolitres against 1,250,000 kL, in the year 1 October to 30 September.
  2. 2GWL118842(2) — the entitlement itselfTaking more than the licence permits is an offence under the Rights in Water and Irrigation Act, not a service failure.
  3. 3L8842/2019/1 condition 23The environmental licence mirrors the volume, so the same take breaches a condition here too.
  4. 4Condition 21 — notify on becoming awareAs soon as practicable, from the timestamp awareness is recorded. The window is stored as null and read as owed now; no number is invented.
  5. ✓The annual water returnDue 2026-10-31, on track. It states the volume taken in each month and the basis of each — which is why the 2 estimates are marked rather than blended.

Every step above is a link to where it is answered: the condition, the return it discharges, and the notification that would run from becoming aware. The flag is the start of that chain rather than a tile on a dashboard, and today it is at the first step and nothing after it is owed.

The entitlement is held on the licence and not on a bore, so PB03’s October take counts against it although condition 23 names only PB01 and PB02. The condition’s wording is kept as the regulator wrote it; the difference is stated here rather than resolved by editing it.

Statutory notification

A countdown against a window, from a timestamp nobody can move.

Why this timestamp is immutable

Window and rule frozen onto the event at 2026-05-22 09:14. A later licence variation cannot move this deadline.

A statutory notification window runs from “became aware”. Missing it is an offence rather than a service failure, so the database refuses an update that moves that timestamp — or the obligation link, because the two together are what the countdown was computed from.

“As soon as practicable” is stored as a null window and read as owed now, never as a blank. The countdown invents no number, and time remaining is truncated rather than rounded — 4 h 59 m never displays as 5 h.

One moment of awareness, two statutory duties, two parts of the regulator.

The licence condition is not the only thing with a clock. The Contaminated Sites Act imposes its own duty on becoming aware of known or suspected contamination — a separate instrument, a separate branch of DWER, a separate lodgement — running from the same timestamp. Discharging one does not discharge the other, and the two are routinely conflated because most products model only the duty written into the licence.

Every statutory duty running from the awareness of 2026-05-22 09:14 AWST.

A separate duty on a separate instrument to a separate part of the regulator, running from the same moment of awareness. Discharging the licence condition does not discharge this one, and the two are commonly confused — which is the reason it is a row rather than a footnote. The Contaminated Sites Act report has not been lodged.

PFOS and PFHxS at 37× the guideline value in groundwater is, on its face, a suspected contaminated site. The duty runs from awareness and carries no fixed window, so it is owed now — and the countdown says exactly that rather than inventing a number or leaving a blank. It sits on the work queue beside the licence notification, not behind it.

Recording that it is with legal discharges nothing. The clock keeps running and the record says so.

Approval and sign-off

Who approved exactly what, and when.

/projects/:projectId/signoff

Sign-off is not a validation state.

Validation says the data is right, and it is made result by result. Approval says a named person accepts responsibility for a document, and it is made once. Collapsing the two means either that approving five hundred results signed a report nobody read, or that signing a report silently approved five hundred numbers.

Three signatures, in three capacities, all dated before the document went out: prepared A. Nakamura 2026-04-24 15:40 · reviewed D. Okafor 2026-04-27 09:18 · approved R. Whitmore 2026-04-27 16:12. A signature dated after lodgement would be a signature on something already gone.

The amendment does not reach it

The staged amendment re-reports 3 results that SNAP-0117 stands on. It changes nothing about this approval. The snapshot is append-only, its digest is unchanged, and the document R. Whitmore signed regenerates from it byte for byte.

That is the reason a signature binds to a snapshot rather than to a project, a period or a query. Bound to any of those, an amendment eighteen months later would silently change what a named person is on record as having accepted — and the person would be the last to know.

What is true, and is stated rather than left to be noticed: 3 of the 228 results beneath this signature have an amended value staged against them. The signature stands; the agreement between the signed document and the standing record is what would move, and it is the “against today’s record” column that carries it.

Superseding a signature is not a thing this product offers. A signature is withdrawn by a further signed act that names it, and both stay readable.

What a new approval would cover

If the amendment were accepted and the 2026 Q1 report reissued, the approval requested would cover:

  • A new snapshot, with its own digestSNAP-0124
  • Results it would stand on228 — 3 at amended values
  • Capacities required again3 — prepared, reviewed, approved
  • Exceedances the document would report7 for the period, down 2
  • The approval of 2026-04-270 changes — it covers SNAP-0117 and continues to
  • Sections needing an author first1 — §6.1 cites a trip that would no longer stand

A requested approval can be withdrawn before it is given. Once given it is a record of what somebody accepted at a moment, and it is never edited — a mistaken approval is answered by a further signed act that names it.

Why is this number what it is?

One result, and everything that produced it — beginning at the bore.

a proposal — the product carries lineage as a panel and the result page, not a route

Proposed as a surface. The engine is complete and nothing shows it.

FR-5, G-09b and the bitemporal survey model are the deepest architectural investment in this product, and “why is this number what it is” is the question no incumbent answers well. There is a lineage graph with single-query answerability underneath, and not one pixel on top of it. This is the highest-value missing screen in the catalogue.

4.8 ng/L PFOS + PFHxS · MW05 · sample WDL-26Q2-003 · collected 2026-05-13 08:40 AWST · certificate YAR-26-0881

The chain starts at the bore, not at the laboratory’s file — 12 hops before the first number.

A senior hydrogeologist reviewing this screen said the chain began too late: it opened on the deliverable, and for a groundwater result the account that has to be given runs location and version → bore and screened interval → programme → field event → field measurements and stabilisation → sample → filtration and preservation → custody transfer → laboratory receipt → analytical batch, method and QC → laboratory result, and only then import, derivation, evaluation and use. Every hop below reads the record that owns it and links to the screen that draws it. Nothing here is a copy: the field half resolves through the bore session, the custody half through the chain of custody, and the laboratory half through the batch.

Explain it

The default, and it stays the default. A chain a practitioner can read aloud to a regulator is the artifact; the graph beside it is a way of seeing the same thing at once.

A graph, deliberately small — and it is not one of the twelve plates.

Two views of one structure, and neither is a second copy of it: both read the same array, so a hop cannot appear in one and not the other. The narrative is what gets read to a regulator; this is what gets looked at when somebody asks what else did that touch. It is drawn in the document rather than as a figure — no scale, no axis, nothing measured — so the frozen chart grammar is not engaged and nothing here is an addition to the approved plate set.

Why this chain and not the metals batch

This result is PFAS. Its certificate is YAR-26-0881 from Yarra Regional Analytical and its batch is YAR-B-118420 — not PAS-WO-268841, which is the dissolved-metals batch this project talks about most because its zinc spike failed.

Chaining a result to the batch that happens to be nearby is the error the chain exists to make impossible. The failed zinc spike qualifies nine results and none of them is this one, and a lineage that implied otherwise would have handed a reviewer a caveat that does not apply and hidden the one that does.

The hop that made this visible is the eleventh: all 38 containers went to Pilbara Analytical Services, and the PFAS certificate is somebody else’s. Pilbara Analytical Services holds no NATA scope for USEPA 1633. The PFAS fraction is subcontracted, and the subcontract laboratory issues its own certificate. One naming convention to read past: PAS-WO-268841 is the submission work order — the number the whole box travels under — and PAS also reports its metals run under it, so the same identifier names this bottle’s physical origin and the metals batch on the QA/QC screen. Yarra Regional issues its own batch, YAR-B-118420, which is why a PFAS result never cites the metals number.

What the chain carries forward rather than closing over

Two things on this chain are unresolved, and both stay visible on it rather than being smoothed away.

Seal number on the second cooler lid. The field record and the laboratory’s receiving form disagree by a digit transposition. Both readings are kept and the chain of custody holds the ways out — none of which is picking one.

The estimated component. PFHxS sits between the method detection limit and the limit of reporting, so it is real and not reliably quantified, and the qualifier carries onto the total. The non-detect rule shows the same total under all three readings of it.

The component that made the wave-6 representation fix necessary: PFHxS at 0.5 < 1.7 < 2.0 ng/L.

The component step read “PFHxS = 1.7 ng/L · detected · LOR 2.0 ng/L”, which is an unqualified detect below the reporting limit — not something a laboratory reports, and a practitioner reading the chain stops there. The three limits are distinct and stay distinct: the MDL is the lowest concentration the method detects with confidence that the analyte is present, the LOR is the lowest it will report as a quantified number, and a value between them is real and imprecise. So the assertion moves to where the glossary puts it — a qualifier, J (USEPA), origin laboratory, meaning estimated — and the detect status stays two-valued. Reported by Yarra Regional on YAR-26-0881 with the J qualifier against the result. The laboratory said it; nobody here inferred it. The qualifier carries onto the derived total, and the non-detect rule shows the same total under all three readings of that component: the number and the confidence move, the outcome does not. What this catalogue does not yet draw is a qualifier channel on the results grid itself, where the total renders with its value and its outcome marks and no qualifier beside them — recorded here rather than left to be noticed.

A second chain, and a question it answers with cannot say

Every chain above ends in a number that can be traced to one bottle from one bore. This one cannot, and that is not a gap in the record — it is the record being accurate about an act somebody took deliberately. A composite sample is made of other samples, so a result on it describes the combination and nothing smaller.

1180 mg/kg Sulfate as SO₄ (1:5 soil:water) · sample WDL-26M5-C02 · collected 2026-05-07 11:05 AWST · certificate PAS2026-04361

12 steps, and not one of them is a derivation.

The chain above turns on a rule with a version, inputs and a recomputable output. This one turns on a compositing scheme — the same word is deliberately not used, because the combining happened to the material before any number existed. There are no component results to keep and nothing to recompute; what the chain carries instead is the increments, their positions and their depth intervals. A product that filed this under derivation would offer to re-derive a number that was never derived.

What criterion was it assessed against?None. 0 of the 5 sets in the library carry a soil or sediment matrix.EvaluationOpen

Why the refusal is a feature of the chain rather than a hole in it

A chain that answered “which increment” would have to invent the answer. There is no rule that recovers it, no statistical treatment that recovers it and no qualifier that expresses it — the information was never created, because the material was mixed before it was measured.

So the chain states the width of what it leaves open instead, in units: with 4 increments, this value is consistent with any one of them reading anything up to 4,720 mg/kg with the rest at zero. That is a computed bound rather than a caution, and it is the honest replacement for an attribution.

This is the one place in the catalogue where a limit does provenance work. Everywhere else a chain gets longer to answer more; here it stops, says why, and names what it would cost to go further.

And what it would cost to go further

The increments were composited at a bench rather than in a bowl, so they still exist — 750 g of each, in a store. 4 analyses instead of the one already run.

Answerable
Yes — by purchase, not by arithmetic
Binding window

Expires
2026-06-03
Left as at 2026-05-24
10 days
After that
The same analysis returns a number with a holding-time qualifier rather than an answer

None of this would be available for the surface composite. Its five increments went into one bowl, and the only way back to a position there is a second mobilisation and a fresh set of holes.

One of the principals above is not the operator’s. lbroadbent@coolibah.example holds a time-bounded Contributor binding through an external engagement, and their act sits on the trail above with the same six fields as every other — same trigger, same transaction id, same before-and-after state.

Nothing marks it as external, and that is the design rather than an omission. The answer comes out of the subject the row already carries: the party owns coolibah.example, the operator’s directory issued the identity, and the trail records what the request arrived as. An is_external column would be a second copy of a fact the customer’s directory owns — set at write time, never re-derived, and wrong the first time somebody joins the operator from the consultancy.

Which is why the filter above is a filter. Attribution is the mechanism; asking the question is a query.

Two questions, two authorities, and they are not the same read

The trail answers both, from the same rows, under different authority.
QuestionWho may ask it
What happened to this row?the history of one result, sample, location or criterionAnyone who can read the row. A trail is readable exactly when its subject is — the read walks back to the row and applies that row’s own scope, so there is no second rule to get wrong and no “no records” answer that really means “not yours”.
What did this principal do, everywhere?one subject, across every project, in a bounded windowAn auditor binding, and only that. It is the one role that is instance-wide by nature, it mints a different kind of authority from a project scope, and a principal without it is refused here rather than handed a narrower answer that looks complete.

So the question at the top of this panel is the second kind. It spans projects by construction — a consultant might hold engagements on two — and an answer narrowed to one project would look like the whole answer while being part of it.

And one thing the trail cannot answer at all: what they read. This is a record of mutations. A sign-in is deliberately not audited — it is the act that establishes the principal, so there is no principal to attribute it to — so “what did they look at” has no row here and no filter will find one. Said out loud because it is the question an operator asks second.

Project settings

What this project is, what it evaluates against, and who can act in it.

/projects/:projectId/settings

What a “project” is for a single-operator customer is not settled, and this screen cannot be finished until it is.

Facility-coextensive — one project per site, always — or a work scope inside a facility, so a closure study and routine compliance monitoring are separate projects over the same bores? The first is simpler and matches every fixture. The second is what a consultancy would need, and the authorisation model already supports it. The screen is drawn against the first reading and says so, rather than quietly choosing.

Identity

Appears in the header, in every export filename and on every report cover. Changing it does not change the URL, which is a UUID.

The facility supplies the area hierarchy every location hangs from. The list is the 2 facilities on this instance, read from the projects that hold them — not a typed list that can name one nobody has.

Every monitoring period, due date and countdown resolves here and never on the server. A quarterly round at a Pilbara bore begins at 16:00 UTC on 31 December — get this wrong and a round that was satisfied reads as missed while a spurious one reads as met.

GDA2020 and WGS84 agree only at epoch 2020.0 and separate by about 7 cm a year. A WGS84 coordinate carries its epoch; one arriving without an epoch is refused rather than assumed.

PFAS is assessed here against ANZG, and ANZG is not the operative PFAS framework

The PFAS National Environmental Management Plan is the agreed ANZ position. It carries its own values, its own derived sums and — the part that matters — a value per receptor, because what protects freshwater ecology is not what protects a drinking-water supply.

Criteria setVersionProtectsPFOS + PFHxSState
PFAS NEMP — freshwater 95%2.0Aquatic ecosystems0.13 µg/Lavailable

ANZG 2018 — 95%2018.1Aquatic ecosystems0.13 µg/Lactive

Assessing against ANZG alone is defensible for freshwater ecology and insufficient the moment a potable or recreational receptor sits downgradient. Because evaluation here is concurrent and every set is versioned, carrying all three is a content decision rather than an architectural one — which is exactly the kind of thing a customer should be able to do without calling anybody.

Applicability

A criteria set is bound by matrix, location group, hydrostratigraphic unit, analyte, fraction and period — not by a global switch. Two sets apply to MW05 concurrently and both outcomes are kept.

G8 promises the customer’s own team can do this without an implementation consultant. Today it is a seed file, and this screen is what that promise actually requires.

What a non-detect contributes to a derived sum

There is deliberately no default, in the schema or in the code. A criteria set without a rule cannot be stored, because the alternative is a value that looks like a decision and is not.

In force: exclude from the sum. Changing it here changes it for this set only — the Licence Table 4 set keeps half-limit substitution, and both answers are kept because two regulators asked two questions.

Why this is a criteria-set field and not a setting

Zero is the dangerous one. Under it every censored total becomes 0.0 ng/L and six results that nobody could assess read as compliant. Nothing on the page would look wrong. That is the same failure as a reporting limit above a criterion rendering as a pass, arriving through a different door.

Under the limit of reporting the same six read as exceedances at 31×, which would raise six statutory notification obligations. One field, and the round is either quiet or a compliance event.

Which is why it is bound to the set: a regulator that specifies half-limit substitution and a regulator that specifies exclusion are both answerable at once, and neither answer is a global preference somebody changed on a Tuesday.

Activation, and what it starts

Activating version 2026.1 on 2026-09-01 → if activated would write:

  • Criteria set versions written1 — 2018.1 is superseded, not deleted
  • Derived totals re-evaluated7
  • Outcomes that change6 — indeterminate becomes exceedance
  • Exceedances raised6, at six locations
  • Notification obligations raised under condition 216 — became-aware set at activation, immutable
  • TARP levels that extend automatically0 — Level 3 names MW05 and extending it is a separate decision
  • Locked periods re-evaluated0 — a rule change evaluates forward
  • Issued reports changed0 — a snapshot is what was issued

Reversible as an evaluation and not as a consequence. Rolling back re-evaluates the seven totals and withdraws the six exceedances; it does not un-lodge a notification that has gone to DWER.

Why activating a criteria set is an approval, not a save

Condition 21 obliges notification as soon as practicable on becoming aware of an exceedance, and the moment of awareness would be this activation. Six statutory clocks, started by a configuration change and running from a timestamp nobody can afterwards move. That is why activating a criteria set is an approval rather than a save.

A became-aware timestamp is immutable at the database and a statutory window runs from it. Missing that window is an offence rather than a service failure — so a configuration change that manufactures six of them belongs behind the same named approval a submission does.

Nothing here re-opens a locked period. The 2026 Q1 round is closed, and a rule change evaluates forward — which is the opposite of the staged amendment, where the data moved under a period already reported and the write has to be decided.

Rollback

Rolling back to version 2018.1 would write:

  • Set version deactivated1 — superseded, and both stay readable
  • Derived totals re-evaluated7
  • Exceedances withdrawn6 — withdrawn, never deleted
  • Notifications un-lodged0 — a lodgement is withdrawn by writing to the regulator
  • Audit records writtenOne per change, appended, attributed

Reversible as an evaluation. An exceedance withdrawn by a rollback is withdrawn and not deleted, and it stays readable with the version that raised it and the version that withdrew it.

What rollback cannot undo

Rollback is drawn as a control rather than left to a database restore, because the question it answers — “we activated the wrong rule on Friday” — is asked on a Monday by somebody who is not a DBA.

A lodged notification is not a row this product owns. It is a document with a regulator, and it is withdrawn by writing to the regulator. Rolling back the rule withdraws the exceedance that obliged it and records that the notification stands — a product that quietly cleared both would have deleted the evidence that a notification was made.

A mapping that was learned wrong, and the correction

Corrected 2025-02-0331 results re-derived

TDS (calc) was mapped to Total dissolved solids (dried) for six months. The laboratory calculates this from electrical conductivity and does not dry it, so every result carried a method it was never measured by.

Correcting the mapping did not edit the results. It superseded them: 31 new results, each pointing at the one it replaced, each carrying the rule version that produced it. The originals are still readable, still attributed, and still show what a report issued in that window was based on.

See the supersession cascadeOpen lineage on one

Correcting Cd-diss → Cadmium (total) would touch:

  • Results re-derived and superseded44
  • Evaluations recomputed88 — two criteria sets
  • Outcomes that would change3
  • Reports already issued that cite them2 — flagged stale, not rewritten
  • Original results deleted0

Reversible as a further correction. Nothing is overwritten — a correction supersedes and reaches back, and the reports that cited the old values stay exactly as they were issued, marked stale.

Never asked twice — but never hidden either

There are three outcomes on a review question, not two, and conflating the last two would put decisions into somebody’s history that they never made.

OutcomeWhose decisionShown as
OutstandingNobody yet — it blocks the commitA question in the queue
Applied from a prior decisionA named person, on a named importApplied, with their name and the import it was made on
Applied by the dictionaryNobody — it is a synonym, not a judgementApplied, attributed to the dictionary

The middle row is the one that has to keep its attribution. “The system did it” and “you did it, eighteen months ago, on the Kurrajong import” are different answers to an auditor, and only one of them is true.

Every profile here is inward, and that is a fact about the mechanism

Why the outward mapping is not a profile

All 3 profiles above are per-laboratory memory: what this laboratory writes, and what this instance decided it means. That shape exists because laboratories differ from each other and drift over time, so the mapping has to be learned, attributed and correctable — and a correction has to reach back over every result it produced.

An outward mapping is none of those things. It is fixed by the receiving party’s specification rather than learned from anyone; it has no per-laboratory dimension, because one file is written for one recipient out of results from several laboratories at once; it produces no results, so there is nothing for a correction to reach back over; and where the evidence for a rename is thin it carries an evidence tier rather than a confidence, because the question is “does a source state this” and not “how sure is the matcher”.

So it lives on the export’s own record, where its 23 rows sit beside the reconciliation they explain. Giving it a profile row here would be a parallel mechanism under this one’s name, which is the failure this screen is otherwise about.

The outward mapping, on the record that applies it

The two mappings, side by side

One boundary, two directions, and almost nothing in common but the word.
Inward — a profileOutward — on the export
Fixed byWhat a laboratory happens to writeThe receiving party’s specification
LearnedYes — by a person or by the dictionary, and it says whichNo. There is nobody to learn it from
Held perLaboratoryTarget format
Scope today3 laboratories, 343 entries1 format, 23 rows
Uncertainty isA confidence, and a low one becomes a questionAn evidence tier, and a thin one writes nothing
Correcting itSupersedes results and reaches backRewrites the next file. Nothing stored moves
A wrong one costsResults carrying a method they were never measured byA recipient reading a number as something it is not

The last row is the one worth sitting with. An inward mistake is recoverable here, because this instance still holds the original file and the supersession machinery to undo what the mapping produced. An outward mistake has already left.

NOx-N is flagged rather than accepted as a synonym for nitrate.

Display unit is not stored unit

A practitioner reading PFAS in ng/L and metals in µg/L on the same crosstab is reading two units, and switching the display to one of them must not touch a single stored value.

Changing this marks every converted cell and states the factor on hover. The stored value, the certificate and the export all keep the laboratory’s own unit.

A converted cell, as it renders
0.0048 µg/L Converted for display from 4.8 ng/L by rule unit-scale v1, ÷ 1000, exact. The stored value is 4.8 ng/L and the export carries that. This conversion is display-only and is not recorded in lineage, because nothing was derived — the number on the record did not move.

Marked as converted, with the rule one hover away. A converted value that looks identical to a reported one is a small lie that compounds.

The conversion that is not a conversion

Depth below ground to elevation above datum looks like a unit change and is not one. It is a derivation against the survey datum in force on the measurement date.

  1. ✓Reading: 15.20 m bgl at MW05, 2026-05-13What the dip meter said. Stored exactly, forever.
  2. ✓Datum in force on 2026-05-13Top of casing 208.11 m AHD, from the resurvey of 2024-03-18. The 2019 survey said 208.42 and applies to readings before that date.
  3. ✓Rule datum-at-date v2208.11 − 15.20 = 192.91 m AHD. Derived at read time and never stored.
  4. 4The same reading, evaluated against 2019’s datum208.42 − 15.20 = 193.22 m AHD. Storing the elevation would have frozen whichever datum happened to be in force the day it was calculated, and a resurvey would silently invalidate years of hydrograph.

“Principals seen” is not a membership count, and the distinction is the design. Strataflow asks the directory which groups is this principal in and never who is in this group — it reads group ids and never their membership — so a roster is a number no request here can produce. What is counted is principals this instance has actually seen, whose membership resolved to the binding at that moment; the auditor binding reads 0 because nobody has used it, not because nobody holds it.

The row above is the only one carrying a party and the only one carrying an end date, and both columns are read from the engagement record rather than stored on the binding — because a role binding in this product is five columns and none of them is either of those. The engagement record says so on its face.

The engagement, and the boundary it rests on

One role is instance-wide, and exactly one can be

Three of the four roles are held within a project: nobody is a contributor in general. Auditor is the exception and the only one — the question it exists to answer, “what did this principal do across the instance”, spans projects by construction, so it is not a scope and cannot be made into one.

The schema is what keeps that honest rather than a convention: a binding is instance-wide if and only if its role is auditor. A project-less Contributor is refused, and so is an auditor pinned to one project. An unscoped grant cannot be arrived at by leaving a field blank and looking like a data-entry slip.

A Reader over “all projects” — which this table used to carry — is therefore not a configuration to be careful with. It is a row the database will not accept, and it is drawn here as the two things it was conflating: a Reader binding on the project, and the auditor authority.

Membership is resolved on every request, not copied at sign-in.

Somebody removed from a directory group loses access on their next request rather than at their next sign-in. Deprovisioning that waits for a session to expire is deprovisioning in name only.

Authorisation in the application; row-level security beneath it.

The repository layer throws when a query is not scoped. The policy beneath it returns zero rows, because a policy cannot safely raise. Two mechanisms doing two jobs, not one wearing two hats.

External-party engagement

A consultancy engaged on one project — what it reaches, what it cannot, and what this product does not have.

a proposal — it would be a child of /instance/access

Proposed, and it draws a seam rather than a feature. External-party access is out of v1.

The product’s own resolution of this question is that it is out of v1 — single operator, single organisation — and that project-scoped row-level security is kept as the seam, so the external-party dimension is added at S8 when a consultancy customer is real. Consultants are named there as people who execute much of this work and as not first-class users in v1. Nothing here reschedules that. What is drawn is the seam holding: a party, an engagement, one binding, and — the part that is the whole point — no new mechanism anywhere beneath it.

Contributor, not Reader, and the reason is worth stating. Validating a result is a write with a principal on it, and drafting a section is a write too. Reader would have been the smaller grant and would have left the trail with nothing to answer “what did the consultants touch” with — the trail records mutations.

One binding, one project, one role from the closed set of four. There is no “external” role and there must not be one: a role says what may be done, and a consultant validating a result is doing the same thing an employee validating a result is doing.

The lifecycle, and where this one is

  1. ✓Proposed — 2026-02-18Scope of work agreed under MOCK-WDL-PO-2214; the group does not exist yet and nothing is reachable.
  2. ✓Active — 2026-03-02The group is created and the binding written. 83 days ago.

  4. 4Ended — 2026-06-19The group is emptied. Access stops at the next request; every row already written keeps its principal.

Four states and only two dates. Expiring is not a fifth thing that happens to an engagement — it is active inside the notice window — so it is computed from 2026-03-02, 2026-06-19 and today rather than stored on a row somebody has to remember to update. A stored state is a state that goes stale on the day it matters.
